title: McConnell is out of rehab, but his absence has stunted a key Republican priority
summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell has been discharged from a rehabilitation facility and will continue recovering at home after a June fall in Kentucky.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses Sen. Mitch McConnell's, R-Ky., update on his health nearly a month after his hospitalization on ‘The Big Weekend Show.’
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., is officially back home after weeks of receiving medical care, but it’s still not clear when he will return to the Senate.

McConnell, in a statement released by his office Thursday afternoon, revealed that he had been "discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home" with his wife, former Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao.

The longtime lawmaker has been absent from the public eye since June after suffering a fall at his Washington, D.C. Late last month, he disclosed that he had been discharged from the hospital, but was not yet "medically cleared" to return to work.
MCCONNELL OUT OF HOSPITAL, STILL NOT 'MEDICALLY CLEARED' TO RETURN TO SENATE
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., on Tuesday, May 12, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"Elaine and I are grateful for the many well-wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff," McConnell said.

"On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business," he continued.
His return to the Senate, however, remains a mystery.

And the upper chamber is still currently in session, mired in negotiations moving at a glacial pace to pass a series of key agenda items before jet-setting from Washington for the rest of August. Whether McConnell returns in early September when the Senate is set to clock back in remains in the air, too.
MCCONNELL'S ABSENCE PUTS TRUMP AGENDA AT RISK AS KENTUCKY SUCCESSION QUESTIONS GROW
Fox News Digital did not immediately receive comment on McConnell's return to the upper chamber.
For weeks, his absence has had little effect on Senate business other than speculation that the day would come when his vote was needed, and he wasn't there.

That changed Thursday morning when Senate Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee, which McConnell is a member of, tried to move a revamped, sweeping farm package through committee. Senate Democrats voted against the package over concerns that the food stamp provisions in the legislation would put more of the cost of the program onto states.
COLLINS DROPS THE HAMMER ON TRUMP'S PICK TO LEAD DOJ, JEOPARDIZING PATH TO CONFIRMATION
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., is still recovering from a fall he suffered at home last month. (Senator Mitch McConnell)
But without McConnell, nor Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., the package failed to survive in committee.
Sen. John Boozman, R-Ark., the chair of the panel, plans to bring the package back up for consideration in September when the Senate returns.

It is also unclear if President Donald Trump's pick to lead the Department of Justice (DOJ), acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, can survive the confirmation process without McConnell. Republicans can only afford to lose one more vote thanks to his absence and Sen. Susan Collins', R-Maine, decision to buck Trump's top prosecutor.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Speculation over McConnell's health, and inconsistent clarity on his condition from his office, sparked an intense and sometimes fantastical rumor mill about the longest-serving Republican leader in Senate history.

It also spurred questions over whether Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, would call a special election to replace him. Beshear argued earlier this week that the Aug. 3 deadline circulating online had no legal bearing on his decision, but did note that without McConnell, Republicans' agenda would suffer.
"Worth a reminder: Right now, there’s one less vote for the SAVE Act, Trump’s war with Iran, or the potential replacement of a SCOTUS justice," Beshear said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Trump allies push to arm president with new tariff weapon to punish countries 'ripping off' America
summary: Sen. Rick Scott's Trade Deficit Elimination Act would give Trump new congressional authority to impose tariffs on countries with trade deficits.
story: FOX Business host Larry Kudlow discusses the impact of the Trump administration's manufacturing policies after the ISM reported its highest manufacturing PMI since 2022 on ‘Kudlow.’

FIRST ON FOX: Just as the Trump administration has refunded billions in tariffs to companies in the U.S., a push is growing in the Senate to give the president sharper, more focused tariff powers across the globe.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., is leading the charge to give President Donald Trump congressional approval for his tariffs, specifically against countries that have longstanding trade deficits with the U.S. after his universal duties were nixed by the Supreme Court.

"Previous generations of Americans gave us an economic superpower; it’s our job to preserve what they built and to leave America better than we found it for our children and grandchildren," Scott told Fox News Digital in a statement.
"That means we can’t let other countries rip us off."
TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

President Donald Trump speaks during a "Make America Wealthy Again" trade announcement event in the Rose Garden at the White House April 2, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images)

Scott’s bill, the Trade Deficit Elimination Act, would effectively create a congressional framework that allows Trump to authorize tariffs where there are trade deficits with the nation’s trade partners that are a detriment to America’s national security, foreign policy interests and economic interests.

It would require the creation of an annual watch list for countries with trade deficits that are identified and compiled by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. That list would deem each country identified as having "trade deficit economies."
From there, Scott’s bill would allow Trump to impose, increase, decrease, suspend or modify tariffs on imports from the listed countries in a bid to eliminate bilateral goods trade deficits.
TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS; NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK

Trump and Greer would still need to seek consultation from Congress, specifically from the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, but aren’t required to get congressional approval for applying duties to listed countries.
It also exempts certain products considered critical to U.S. supply chains, U.S. supply chains, national security or where alternative sources are unavailable.

"In recent years, our trading partners have taken advantage of access to American markets while unfairly crowding American products out of their own countries," Scott said. "Decline is a choice, and President Trump is taking action to restore American prosperity."
DEMOCRATS CHEER SUPREME COURT MOVE BLOCKING TRUMP TARIFFS — DESPITE PAST SUPPORT FOR TRADE DUTIES
Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., in the Senate Subway during a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., March 14, 2025. (Allison Robbert/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Scott’s announcement of the bill comes just a day after the Trump administration refunded $100 billion in tariff revenue collected during the president’s "liberation day" explosion of duties across the globe.
Trump issued those tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). But the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that he didn’t have the authority to do so.

Scott’s bill has so far picked up senators Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., and Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., as co-sponsors, and is a separate authority entirely from the IEEPA. It creates a new power, with congressional teeth, under Article 1, Section 8 directly targeting foreign commerce.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Trade should be fair, not one-sided, and it’s refreshing to have a president who isn’t afraid to hold our trading partners accountable," Cramer said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "This bill gives President Trump and Ambassador Greer tools to address trade deficits, keep critical supply chains intact, and achieve better trade agreements for American farmers, ranchers, manufacturers and workers."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Reporter's Notebook: Summer ends, but the Senate's fall crunch begins
summary: The Senate faces a daunting list, including Todd Blanche's confirmation, government funding, the SAVE America Act and college sports NIL regulation.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram has the latest on the Senate approaching recess as President Donald Trump urges the SAVE Act to pass on 'Special Report.'
It may be summer. But fall is consuming the United States Senate.
Bipartisan lawmakers are trying to avoid a government shutdown.
"The fiscal year begins Oct. 1 each year," said Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa. "This resolution keeps the government open for business."

The House approved an interim spending bill in July to keep the government funded through Dec. 4. But bipartisan senators are trying to duck yet another protracted government shutdown odyssey, like last year’s 43-day exercise.
HOUSE GOP VOTES TO PUNT GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BATTLE TO AFTER NOVEMBER MIDTERMS
A shutdown occurs when Congress and the president fail to sign into law 12 appropriations bills to continue providing funding for government operations. (Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty Images)
"I look forward to passing this bill in the next few days," said Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.

The measure funds the government with a fiscal Band-Aid through Dec. 11 – well after the midterms. But Democratic buy-in is paramount. The main reason the government closed last fall was because Senate Democrats refused to provide votes to break a filibuster on the GOP plan. Democrats protested a lapse in Obamacare subsidies – and hoped to underscore to voters that Republicans were vulnerable on healthcare. Now Democrats are on board. The Senate curbed a filibuster on the bill with a vote tally of 89-4. The question is when the Senate will pass the bill. And what happens when senators send this to the House.
"We want to fund the government and avoid a shutdown," said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.
Ironically, funding the government may be the easiest thing before the Senate right now.

There are all sorts of lists out there. Santa’s list. Hollywood’s blacklist. Craigslist. And bucket lists. But no list is more daunting than what the Senate is trying to accomplish over the next few days. And truth be told, the Senate might not check much off its list at all.

Senators are bewildered about what the plan is over the next few days. Many hope to escape Washington. Those running for re-election are anxious to head home and campaign as control of the Senate swings in the balance.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., emerged from the Senate Republican weekly luncheon on Tuesday, mystified about what the legislative traffic may look like.
"If there is a plan, they are doing a good job of hiding it," said Kennedy. "I learned nothing in that meeting."
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE'S FINAL SPRINT PUTS SAVE AMERICA ACT AND IRAN FUNDING IN PLAY
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., speaks to reporters as he leaves the Senate Republicans' lunch meeting in the U.S. Capitol on June 25, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
Kennedy posited that "maybe it's because our leadership doesn't know."

In no particular order, here are some of the big ticket items the Senate hopes to rifle through over the coming days: A bill to sanction Russia, named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C. Confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general. Handle a budget resolution so the GOP can prep a filibuster-free bill to restock military munitions because of the war in Iran and maybe approve parts of the SAVE America Act. Fund the government. Greenlight a slate of nominations unrelated to Blanche. Advance a bill to regulate college sports and the use of NIL (for name, image and likeness). Perhaps reauthorize FISA, the nation’s top terrorism prevention program. And finally, establish a framework for cryptocurrency. The last one is the least likely.
"I feel like we're trying to put 20 pounds of potatoes in a 10-pound bag," said Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., on Fox.

Confirming Blanche is probably the biggest priority for Republicans. But it’s unclear if Blanche has the votes. Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, came around over the weekend after they received assurances from Blanche that the anti-weaponization fund was dead. Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Bill Cassidy, R-La., huddled with Blanche late Wednesday. With former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., out and Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, a nay on Blanche, Republicans can only lose one more of their own and still confirm him.

Ironically, the hallmark of President Donald Trump’s legislative agenda, the SAVE America Act — which requires proof of citizenship to vote — is the one thing the Senate might not tackle. But GOP senators could present the president half a loaf with some voter ID mandates and election security. In short, the Senate won’t cancel its summer recess to pass the SAVE America Act.
"I think there’s nothing more important than the Save America Act. I think they should stay," said Trump.
Even the Senate’s newest member wants to stay in Washington — even though she faces a primary next week.
TRUMP'S VOTER ID BILL CATCHES UNLIKELY BREAK AS MCCONNELL REMAINS SIDELINED
Sen. Darline Graham Nordone, R-S.C., participates in a ceremonial swearing-in at the Old Senate Chamber on July 14 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
"What's up with recess, anyway? Who gets a month off from work? I think we should stay up there and work and get it done," said Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C.
Some Republicans dared their colleagues to thwart the bill.

"If you're going to oppose something, you've got to earn it on the floor as opposed to this kind of kabuki theater we do right now where you just give a thumbs up or a thumbs down," said Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo.

Thune – who often doesn’t see eye-to-eye with the president – dismissed the push for the SAVE America Act. It’s about the math. Thune lacks votes to pass it. In fact, the Senate’s already blocked that bill twice.

"It seems to me some days that I'm the only one here who can count to 50 in this town. But we don't have the votes to get rid of the filibuster. And we aren't flipping 10 Democrats to vote for the SAVE America Act," said Thune.
But even if they won’t vote yes, some Democrats commiserate with Thune.
GOP RIFT GROWS AS THUNE HITS BRAKES ON TRUMP'S ELECTION BILL TO AVERT SHUTDOWN

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, joined by Sen. Tim Scott, speaks to reporters following the weekly Senate Republican policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"The votes don't exist and some of our colleagues just don't know how to count sometimes," said Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M.
Political observers wonder if it was risky for Senate Republicans to promise the SAVE America Act to party loyalists – but fail to deliver.
But Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., disagreed with that argument.
"I don't think we overpromised. I think we wished it would work," said Tuberville.
"There wasn't a plan? This was a wish?" I inquired.
"There's nothing certain up here. I've learned that in six years," replied Tuberville. "I wish we could get this done for the people of Alabama."
"There's that word, again: wish," I said to Tuberville.
PRESIDENT TRUMP PUSHES LAWMAKERS ON LEGISLATION AS 'PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT' HANGS ON BY A THREAD
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., speaks to reporters as he returns to his office at the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

There’s a possible breakthrough on a bill to regulate college sports and fundamentally alter compensation structures for student-athletes. President Trump is pushing lawmakers to vote on the plan after the SEC and Big 10 signed off on the legislation.
"NIL or whatever it is, is very close to getting solved. And we have a bipartisan deal as of right now," said the president.
At best, the college sports bill could score a procedural vote – which is significant. But there’s still much to hash out.
"It's not ready," said Kennedy. "I think many senators still have questions."
Yours truly told Kennedy that the bill "seemed pretty dense when I read it."
The Louisiana Republican agreed.
"It’s dense as hell," said Kennedy. "That's a legal term."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
This Senate agenda is pretty dense. And maybe getting it all done now is a wish. Especially in such a short period.
No matter what, summer is winding down in the Senate. It will soon be fall. Both on the calendar and on Capitol Hill.
And many senators are just wishing they could go home.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Democrats targeting 12 additional red districts in midterms push to retake House
summary: The DCCC is targeting 12 additional deep-red House districts, including seats held by Lauren Boebert and Mike Lawler, as Democrats eye midterm flips.
story: Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Rep. Suzan DelBene speaks one-on-one with Fox News Digital about the House Democrats’ midterm playbook.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) announced 12 additional red U.S. House districts the organization intends to target in November, on top of the 46 it had already designated as possible flips.

The DCCC identified seats held by Reps. Lauren Boebert of Colorado, French Hill of Arkansas, Mike Flood of Nebraska and several other Republicans as being "in play" for Democrats in the midterm elections.

"House Democrats are expanding the battlefield deep into Trump terrain because we have a winning message focused on fighting for an Affordable America," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement on Wednesday.

"At the same time, MAGA Republicans who historically have considered themselves ‘safe’ have let down the people they were elected to represent, passing disastrous policies that are crushing working families and our communities," DelBene added. "Democrats are going to win in November and make Hakeem Jeffries the next Speaker of the House."
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME
Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., departs following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 15, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to the DCCC for more insight into why certain candidates were listed as vulnerable.
Many of the Republicans the DCCC has previously targeted for ouster are candidates that have been embroiled in scandals in recent months.
One such example is Rep. Max Miller of Ohio's 7th District, whose ex-wife Emily Moreno has accused him of physically abusing both her and their young daughter.
Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, attends a Ways and Means Committee hearing in Longworth building on June 4, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
OHIO GOP FAMILY FEUD EXPLODES AS SEN BERNIE MORENO CALLS ON REP MAX MILLER TO RESIGN
Another Republican congressman seen by the DCC as ripe for removal is Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey's 7th District.
Kean was absent from Congress for nearly four months and in that time, he missed 140 roll call votes in the House. He returned on June 30 and announced that he had been diagnosed with depression.
Rep. Mike Lawler of New York's 17th District is also named on the DCCC's list of vulnerable Republicans.
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., marches in a July Fourth parade along the Walkway of Heroes and Independence Avenue on July 4, 2026, in Tappan, New York. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Lawler has been in the crosshairs of Democrats since he narrowly defeated centrist Democrat Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022. In 2024, Lawler handily fended off a challenge from Mondaire Jones, the ex-congressman who used to represent the 17th District.

The district includes all of Rockland and Putnam counties, which President Donald Trump won by double digits in the 2024 election. However, it also includes parts of Westchester County, which overwhelmingly voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Burrito debate rips open GOP civil war on affordability: ‘We will lose, and deserve it’
summary: A college student's complaint about a $20 burrito sparked a fierce GOP debate on affordability, even drawing in JD Vance and Rep. Dan Crenshaw.
story: Fox News’ Madeleine Rivera and Rep. Mark Alford, R-Mo., join Fox News Live to discuss the affordability crisis' impacts on food and real estate, GOP warnings of socialism, and a CCP-linked trailer park near a secret US base.
A debate over whether a burrito should cost $20 has ignited a Republican civil war over affordability and the party’s appeal to younger voters ahead of the midterm elections.
The clash began Wednesday when Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet shared a college student’s complaint that basic purchases have become prohibitively expensive.

"​​One of our TPUSA college students gave me his take on affordability: ‘A burrito shouldn’t cost $20,’" he posted to X on Wednesday. "Yeah, a lot of this is a hangover from Covid and Biden-era inflation, but the lived experience is the same: It just feels like basic things cost too much."

Fiscal conservatives took the position that food is generally affordable if one cooks for themselves and that purchasing a $20 burrito should be considered an occasional luxury. Those aligned with the populist wing of the GOP, meanwhile, argued that traditional conservatives are out of touch with the youth and that the Republican Party faces electoral peril unless it can meaningfully address affordability concerns.
NEW POLL COMPLICATES VANCE’S STATUS AS TRUMP’S LIKELY 2028 HEIR APPARENT

Andrew Kolvet, producer of 'The Charlie Kirk Show,' speaks during the public memorial service for Charlie Kirk at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, on Sep.t 21. (Patrick t. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)

"Just hearing about this dumb $20 burrito debate so just thought I’d make the losers on social media angry before going to bed," Rep. Dan Crenshaw wrote on Wednesday night. "Stop whining, get a job, eat Ramen like the rest of us did in college, on a budget with 4 roommates. The market doesn’t care what you think something ‘should’ cost."
RealClearInvestigations senior writer Mark Hemingway, however, said that such an approach to affordability concerns could prove toxic to the GOP.
'IT'S A MESS': GOP TURNS ON HOUSE CONSERVATIVES AS VOTER ID BLOCKADE STALLS TRUMP'S AGENDA
A Chipotle logo is displayed outside their restaurant on Feb. 24, 2025, in San Diego, California. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

"Andrew [Kolvet] is absolutely right about this, and pundits deflecting because you can cook at home cheaper are not helping," he said. "Eating a burrito once in a while should not be an aspirational lifestyle, for crying out loud."

"The comments saying stick to the dining hall or buy microwaveable burritos are missing the ENTIRE point," Defense of Freedom Institute spokeswoman Angela Morabito said. "If the Right's ‘solution’ to the affordability crisis is telling people to eat worse food, we will lose, and we will deserve it."

Chipotle burritos generally run between about $9 and $12 depending on location, with cheaper restaurants, such as Taco Bell, offering more affordable options. Some fiscal conservatives also pointed out that young people can save money by preparing meals at home.

"A burrito only costs $20 when you buy it on Door Dash because you’re too lazy to walk over to Chipotle or Taco Bell (where you can get one for $3.99)," Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen wrote in response to a populist arguing that the GOP could surrender ground to socialists by not addressing affordability. "When I graduated I lived on ramen noodles, had two roommates, and worked two jobs. I didn’t whine about affordability, I worked hard so I could one day afford a better life."
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Vice President JD Vance attends a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland on July 31, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)
Vice President JD Vance then added to the debate, responding to Thiessen.
"I'm surprised to hear Mark say this. If you've ever met him in person, it's quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito," the vice president wrote.
Bradley Devlin, politics editor at the Daily Signal, claimed that some involved in the burrito discourse were ignorant of financial sacrifices he says are quite common among young people.

"The Burrito Discourse has exposed that so people with thoughts on the youths have not spoken to one in years," he wrote. "They do not expect to live off delivered food from bespoke restaurants and live on their own. I don’t know a single 20 something who lives on their own right now. Having a college degree and two jobs is around the highest it’s ever been. ‘The college premium’ has dried up."

Others responded to the debate in jest.
"I don't care for burritos," Daily Wire host Michael Knowles posted.

title: 'Fake' moderate Talarico's Texas surge tests Paxton in fight to hold crucial GOP Senate seat
summary: Ken Paxton says he's confident Texans will reject James Talarico once they learn about his record on border security, energy and social issues.
story: Republican Senate candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton addresses his Democratic opponent’s current lead in the race and his plan to get his message to voters.

EXCLUSIVE: As Democrats salivate over an elusive statewide victory in Texas, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton says he is undeterred by recent polling showing his Democratic opponent James Talarico holding a slim lead.

Democrats believe this is their moment to finally flip Texas blue after decades of frustrated efforts. Such an upset would be devastating for the GOP’s chances of retaining a Senate majority. Speaking with Fox News Digital after a rally in Houston, Paxton said Talarico’s current lead is "not surprising" given "we were three months behind" after his primary runoff with incumbent Sen. John Cornyn.

"He had three months to fundraise. So, he's been spending $2 million a week to gain that advance," Paxton said. Despite this, Paxton, who currently serves as Texas’ attorney general, said that, come Election Day, he is confident Texans will reject the "real James Talarico" when they hear about his record. Talarico, a state Democratic lawmaker, has a history of controversial statements, including previously asserting that "God is nonbinary," that there are six sexes, and calling it "existential" to reduce meat consumption to fight climate change.

"I do not believe a poll that tells me that, ‘We don't care what he believes. We don't care that he voted for a state income tax. We don't care that he wanted to trans children. We don't care that he's against the oil and gas industry. We don't care that he voted against every border security bill,’" Paxton continued. "I don't believe a poll that says Texans don't care about those issues. I've done enough polling; I've been in this long enough that that's just not true."
JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY'

Left: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a press conference on July 22, 2026, in Austin, Texas. Right: Attorney General Ken Paxton at a campaign event on Aug. 4, 2026, in Allen, Texas. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images; Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
This comes as both candidates continue to crisscross the Lone Star State to get their message out to voters.

A recent Fox News poll of Texas voters showed Talarico with a within-margin-of-error lead in the race, 51% to 48%. Talarico held a slightly wider lead among extremely motivated and extremely interested voters, 53% to 47%, according to the poll. Critically, the Fox News poll found that 59% of Texas voters indicated they are concerned about Paxton’s character while just 47% indicated they are concerned about Talarico being "too extreme" for Texas.

Paxton accused Talarico of "trying to mislead people about who he is" by masking a far-left "socialist" agenda while running as a moderate. He said Talarico has "changed all his positions on pick an issue, whether it's boys in girls’ sports, or meat, or trans-ing kids."
"All of his positions suddenly changed for the general election [but] we have his votes, and we have his words, and those will be out," he said.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Talarico campaign for comment and did not receive a response before publication.
JOE ROGAN WARNS LIBERALS AGAINST TRYING TO TURN TEXAS BLUE, SAYS IT WOULD WRECK THE STATE'S 'DELICATE BALANCE'
Talarico held a general election kick-off event in Houston the day after Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton won the GOP's Senate nomination. (Peter Pinedo/Fox News Digital)

While he acknowledged that many Texas voters have not heard his messaging on Talarico’s controversial views, he pointed out during his rally that Talarico has been aided by an influx of cash from out of state, particularly California.

Fox News Digital reported in June that donors from outside Texas accounted for roughly 50% of the funds Talarico received during the final stretch of the first quarter of 2026. During the same time period, Paxton, meanwhile, received about 25% of his cash from outside the state.

Still, the fundraising difference is stark. The Texas Tribune reported in late July that the latest quarterly Federal Election Commission filings show Talarico outraised Paxton by a more than three-to-one margin, $31.6 million to $9.3 million.

Paxton, however, appeared unbothered by all of this, pointing to how Talarico has had the advantage of several months to focus his attacks. While polling suggests the Texas GOP remains divided after the particularly messy Senate primary, Paxton said, "Primaries are like that for Democrats and Republicans" and "we are coming together."
TALARICO TOUTS TEXAS ROOTS AS OUT-OF-STATE CASH POWERS SENATE CAMPAIGN
Attorney General Ken Paxton during the Texas GOP convention in the George R. Brown Convention Center in Houston, June 12, 2026. (Melissa Phillip/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)

As he travels the state, he said he will continue highlighting the "stark difference" between him and Talarico. Meanwhile, the attorney general said he will be keeping his pitch focused on affordability and cutting regulations.

"We know that Texans need help; we know that Americans need help. That's why I'm suggesting, and what I'm proposing is a first-time homebuyers’ $50,000 tax deduction, I'm proposing a $25,000 a year deduction for medical expenses including insurance premiums for everyone in the family. The child tax credit being doubled, the Trump accounts being continued. And then a $5,000 healthy living deduction so that you can pay for gym expenses and nutrition programs, sports activities, and even doctor-prescribed GLP-1," he said.

"We're still three months out," Paxton continued. "And I know that when we put our resources together, when we get there, we will be able to highlight things and once the voters know the real James Talarico, not the fake one that's running right now… people will get to decide for themselves."

"Do we want a socialist Democrat in Texas?" he asked. "I think the answer is going to be absolutely not."
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Socialist victories show Dems' descent down 'deadly path of communism,' Johnson warns
summary: Mike Johnson warns Democrats are heading toward communism as DSA-backed candidates like Abdul El-Sayed topple establishment figures in key races.
story: Rising socialist momentum in the Democratic primaries threatens party unity as far-left candidate Abdul El-Sayed narrowly wins 48.5% of the vote to defeat moderate Haley Stevens in Michigan.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is arguing that Democrats are descending a dark path as a socialist insurgency on the left continues to notch victories against the party's establishment.

Republicans on the campaign trail have seized on the raging civil war within the Democratic Party, warning that a recent slate of wins by candidates linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is pushing one of the United States' two main political parties much further left than the vast majority of Americans are comfortable with.

"Right now, it's a contrast election for everybody," Johnson said during a campaign stop in Arizona. "They've got to make a decision that they want to continue with common sense, growth and opportunity, or they want to go to this dark down, dangerous, deadly road of communism."
DEMOCRATS TARGET MORE GOP HOUSE SEATS AFTER SOCIALIST VICTORIES ROCK LEFT-WING PRIMARIES

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., from left, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., speak during the "The People v. The Powerful" campaign event at the Detroit Opera House in Detroit on July 18, 2026. (Nic Antaya/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
He said it was a choice "between common sense and crazy."

Johnson and other House GOP leaders are crisscrossing the country visiting districts represented by vulnerable Republican lawmakers and other areas where the GOP believes it has a shot of winning in November.
The Louisiana Republican made a similar pitch earlier this week during a town hall for Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., who is facing a well-connected and well-funded primary opponent on Thursday night.

"Could we've imagined even 10 years ago, if somebody told us that on the two hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the greatest nation in the history of the world, in the midterm, in the fall of 2026, we'd be in a contest to determine whether we're going to maintain our constitutional republic — the greatest nation in history — or go down this dark, dangerous, deadly road to communism?" Johnson said.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, speaks to members of the media after a meeting with House Republicans at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. on July 15, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

It's likely going to be a line the speaker often uses during his appearances ahead of the midterms, with Republicans writ large seeing a boon in the far-left candidates toppling establishment Democrats.

The left's socialist insurgency scored significant wins earlier this week when Dr. Abdul El-Sayed beat out establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., for the Democratic nomination for Michigan's open Senate seat.

Elsewhere in the state, Sunrise Movement co-founder William Lawrence defeated former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink for the Democratic nomination to face Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., in what will be one of the most closely watched battleground races of November.
Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, left, Sen. Bernie Sanders, center, and House candidate William Lawrence, right, at a rally in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Andrew Roth/Sipa USA via Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Among the DSA's policy positions is a call for eliminating the U.S. Senate and extending voting rights to noncitizens and felons on a national level.

Republicans are fighting an uphill battle to defy decades of political convention to keep and even expand their razor-thin majority in the House, but GOP leaders are betting on more far-left victories to give their party a better shot.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Loophole forcing release of detained illegal immigrants targeted by Senate GOP
summary: Sen. Katie Britt's bill targets a 2001 Supreme Court loophole allowing detained illegal immigrants to be released after six months if no country accepts them.
story: Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., and a host of Senate Republicans are pushing legislation that would close a loophole that allows detained illegal immigrants to be released back into the U.S. if their home country won't take them back.
FIRST ON FOX: Senate Republicans are pushing to close a decades-old immigration loophole they say was heavily abused by the Biden administration.
The effort, led by Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., would prevent detained illegal immigrants from being released back into the U.S. in the event that their home countries would not accept their return.

Britt told Fox News Digital that her bill, the Keeping Our Communities Safe Act, would cinch tight the loophole that was created in 2001 when the Supreme Court ruled that illegal immigrants could be released from detention after six months if no country accepted them for deportation.
FAUCI HELD IN CONTEMPT AS COVID CELLPHONE LANDS IN HANDS OF SENATE INVESTIGATORS

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., attends the confirmation hearing for acting Attorney General Todd Blanche before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill on July 15, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

"Ultimately, we want to create pathways for these people to go back to the country they came from," Britt said. "But just because we can't get a country to comply does not mean that that person should get to roam free in the United States of America."

"They should be there in detention until we're able to find them a pathway back to their country," she continued. "So this loophole was obviously exploited a great deal in the Biden administration, and what we're doing is making sure that we are putting forth legislation that closes it once and for all."
Over two decades ago, the court ruling limited the federal government’s authority to detain illegal immigrants and instilled a time frame that a noncitizen could remain detained.
TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS

Once that six-month period has elapsed and there is no likelihood of removal, the government is tasked with presenting evidence that removal is still likely and on the table. But if they can’t, the detainee has to be released under supervision.

Britt’s bill targets two sections of the Immigration and Nationality Act, a 1950s-era law that has undergirded the nation’s immigration laws for decades, to expand the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) authority to detain criminal aliens, deny bonds to criminal aliens, and generally limit the availability of bonds unless an illegal immigrant can establish by clear and convincing evidence that they’re not a flight risk or a risk to another person or the community.
It would also allow for extensions of detention in a number of cases, including in cases where an alien is a threat to national security or has committed an aggravated felony or violent crime.
DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE
Exterior view of the Otay Mesa Immigration Customs Enforcement detention center in San Diego.  (Getty)
The bill has been circulating in Congress since 2011. Britt also tried to get it passed during the Biden administration.

The legislation has 11 Senate Republicans on board as co-sponsors, including Sens. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, Ted Cruz, R-Texas, Deb Fischer, R-Neb., Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., Roger Marshall, R-Kan., Jim Risch, R-Idaho, and Mike Rounds, R-S.D.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Joe Biden and Kamala Harris allowed millions of illegals to INVADE our country — and now law-abiding Americans are paying the price," Tuberville said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "We need to do everything we can to deport every single one of these criminals."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: House GOP launches probe into 5 major labor unions over Dem spending despite MAGA membership base
summary: GOP lawmakers demand financial records from UAW, United Steelworkers, SMART-TD, BLET and BMWED over alleged political spending and lavish perks.
story: Rep. Tim Walberg, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital the investigation is focused on transparency and protecting rank-and-file union members.

FIRST ON FOX: The Republican-led House Committee on Education and Workforce is demanding financial records from five of the nation's largest labor unions over allegations that union leaders used funds to support Democratic candidates and progressive causes while spending millions on lavish perks.

In letters obtained by Fox News Digital and sent Thursday, the lawmakers on the committee requested financial records dating back to January 2023 from the United Auto Workers (UAW), United Steelworkers (USW), SMART Transportation Division (SMART-TD), Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen (BLET), and Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees Division (BMWED).

"Unions are supposed to be representing workers for their best interests on the job site, for their future goals that they have, and to work together in a commonality that speaks for, I think, in general, all of the workers combined and not just select portions of it," Rep. Tim Walberg, R-Mich., who also serves as the chairman of the House Committee on Education and Workforce, told Fox News Digital.

"When we see funds that have been used by multiple unions for highly political purposes, and you begin to see that the rank and file aren't following along with the same political funding purposes of union leadership, common sense says you ought to take a look at it."
EXPLOSIVE REPORT UNEARTHS PROMINENT UNION MONEY TRAIL LABELED A 'STUNNING BETRAYAL' OF MAGA MEMBERS
President Donald Trump takes questions from the media during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on July 21, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Multiple reports cited in the letters, including previous Fox News Digital reporting on BMWED's political spending, allege union leaders spent millions supporting Democratic candidates and progressive causes while also spending heavily on conferences, travel, entertainment and other expenses.
The UAW had the highest reported totals, with nearly $95 million in political spending and nearly $146 million spent on travel and entertainment.

The requests also seek records on lobbying, executive pay, travel, entertainment and conference expenses, along with member complaints, ethics and audit policies, transfers to larger labor organizations, and the use of union funds to cover expenses for spouses, family members, guests or political allies.

The lawmakers argue there is a growing disconnect between union leadership and members, saying many rank-and-file workers have "increasingly supported President Trump and other Republican candidates in recent election cycles."

"I think it comes down to the leader's own self-interest," Walberg said. "That could be political interest, or that could be self-aggrandizement, or in certain cases looks like for monetary purposes, for their own personal benefit."

In the letters, the lawmakers said that workers "deserve transparency regarding how their dues are spent, the extent to which union leadership consults members before endorsing candidates or engaging in political activities, and whether differing viewpoints within the union are being respected."
FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY
Rep. Tim Walberg of Michigan speaks during a House Workforce and Education Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on June 5, 2025. (Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images)
Walberg said the committee is examining how some unions spend dues collected under "mandatory membership policies."

"We have responsibility in our committee for oversight on what goes on in the workplace, what goes in those that represent workers in the work place on both sides of the equation, whether it's the employer or the union," he said.
But Walberg said union leaders still face questions about serving workers' best interests.
"There have been union leaders who have gone to jail and certainly been prosecuted over misuse of funds," he said. "There seems to be indication that that still is going on in certain major unions."

Insisting "this is not to be a partisan political motivated effort," Walberg said the committee's role is oversight and that evidence uncovered during the investigation could still be referred to the Justice Department.

"We do not have prosecutorial powers," he said. "We can't put anybody in jail. We can call for information, and ultimately call for union leadership to come before our committee and answer questions."
SOURCES CORROBORATE WHISTLEBLOWER CLAIMS OF CORRUPTION, QUID PRO QUO CULTURE INSIDE POWERFUL NYC UNION
Supporters hold up signs during a campaign event for President Donald Trump at Xtreme Manufacturing on Sept. 13, 2020, in Henderson, Nevada. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

"We are glad to see Congress is taking a hard look at this—union workers deserve the full truth on how their dues are spent, and whether that spending actually reflects their values," American Accountability Foundation President Tom Jones told Fox News Digital.
The unions were asked to respond by Aug. 17, with the UAW receiving a separate Aug. 18 deadline.

"The committee will continue examining whether current labor law adequately protects workers from political coercion and whether additional transparency requirements are warranted," according to the letters.

The letters added that the unions' responses will assist "in determining whether any legislative changes are warranted," arguing unions have a legal duty to fairly represent members and that workers "should not be compelled to subsidize political advocacy fundamentally at odds with their beliefs or interests."
Walberg said the investigation is "for a purpose," one he hopes will hold union leaders accountable.

"I hope that will be very apparent and transparent that we are concerned about the rank-and-file union member who in most cases had no choice about their contributions but should have a clear understanding and the ability to react to that understanding about how their funds are being used for political, cultural, you name it, purposes and have their union leadership brought to light," he said.

In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, SMART-TD spokesperson Dan Banks said that regarding the union's finances, labor organizations already face "extensive federal reporting and disclosure requirements" and urged the committee to "focus its efforts on legislation that meaningfully improves the lives and working conditions of American workers."
In another statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for the UAW said the union received the letter and is reviewing it, and "will cooperate with the Committee's inquiry."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital also reached out to the UAW, USW, BLET and BMWED for comment. BMWED declined to comment, while the other unions did not respond by publication.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: FBI’s ‘clever’ Trump-Russia probe code name ignites suspicion something deeper was at play
summary: Jeff Clark alleges the FBI deliberately misspelled its Trump-Russia probe name "Oxferd C0mma," using a zero to foil FOIA requests and hide records.
story: Article III Project president Mike Davis discusses the DOJ subpoena of former FBI Director James Comey in an investigation into a ‘grand conspiracy’ to undermine Trump’s presidency on 'The Ingraham Angle.'

The White House on Wednesday released declassified FBI memos showing the bureau investigated whether President Donald Trump’s firing of James Comey was tied to Russia under the oddly spelled code name "Oxferd Comma," fueling speculation that the misspelling was intentional.
Former acting Assistant Attorney General Jeff Clark alleged the code name was deliberately altered to make records of the investigation harder to find.

"The FBI under James Comey and Christopher Wray was hopelessly corrupt. To penalize President Trump’s firing of Comey, they created a ridiculous investigation into Trump on the theory he was a witting or unwitting Russian agent," Clark, who serves as vice president of litigation at the Oversight Project, told Fox News Digital.

"They called it OXFERD C0MMA (note the zero for the second ‘o’ and the misspelling of the University). The FBI managers thought this was clever. They imagined themselves as Blofeld in a James Bond movie deviously defeating the Freedom of Information Act," Clark added, referring to the James Bond supervillain.
TRUMP ALLY DIGENOVA TAPPED TO LEAD DOJ PROBE INTO BRENNAN OVER RUSSIA PROBE ORIGINS
Acting Assistant Attorney General Jeffrey Clark speaks during a news conference at the Justice Department on Oct. 21, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Yuri Gripas-Pool/Getty Images)
Clark explained on social media that he "consulted with a document expert" who concluded the first "o" in "Comma" was actually a zero – further obscuring the probe's name.

Investigators on the "Oxferd Comma" case sought to determine whether Trump was "directed by, controlled by, and/or coordinated activities with, the Russian Federation in a manner constituting a threat to the national security of the United States and/or a violation of federal criminal statutes," according to a May 16, 2017, FBI memo.

Trump fired Comey in May 2017, with the White House initially citing Comey’s handling of the Hillary Clinton email investigation. The FBI opened the "Oxferd Comma" probe days later to examine whether the firing was connected to Russia.

"Additionally, let me speculate that James Comey was well-known by his associates as liking Oxford commas, so they named the operation (clearly motivated by revenge in response to Trump firing Comey) as a hommage (Fr.) to their beloved Comey," Clark added. "But that doesn’t explain why it was deliberately misspelled as 'Oxferd.'"

Clark, who served in Trump’s first administration, argued that the misspelling could have made it more difficult for anyone searching for records related to the operation. He suggested that a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request using the correct spelling might not have returned the relevant documents, potentially allowing the FBI to say that no responsive records had been found.
LEFT-WING GROUP CHASES PROOF OF KASH PATEL'S ALLEGED 'EXCESSIVE DRINKING' AS DEMS EYE FBI DIRECTOR'S OUSTER
The logo of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Wray, Comey and the White House for comment.
"It should be investigated as an obstruction of justice. You know, some real obstruction of an official proceeding," Clark posted to X.
The unusual spelling also drew attention on social media, where users resurfaced a 2017 Comey post about Oxford commas.
"Check the actual cover. I’m all about Oxford commas," Comey wrote in a 2017 X post about his then-forthcoming memoir, "A Higher Loyalty: Truth, Lies, and Leadership."
OBAMA-ERA ATTORNEY FLIPS SCRIPT ON COMEY INDICTMENT NAYSAYERS WITH WARNING NOT TO BURY DOJ YET
An FBI agent and a Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) officer arrest a man near the White House in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 15, 2025. (Yasin Ozturk /Anadolu via Getty Images)
The FBI did not directly address the code name when asked by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

"The weaponization that occurred against President Trump under prior regimes was inexcusable and wholly un-American. Director Patel himself was the lead investigator who originally exposed the disgraceful Crossfire Hurricane scandal – and as Director, he has released over 40,000 pages of documents to the public exposing similar malfeasance from former FBI leadership – a three fold increase from both his predecessors combined," Ben Williamson, assistant director of the FBI’s Office of Public Affairs, said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As we’ve said repeatedly: any individual who is found to have acted unethically or engaged in weaponization has been or will be fired from the Bureau and held accountable under the law," Williamson added.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: WATCH: GOP split over Rand Paul’s DOJ strategy in Fauci contempt push
summary: Sen. Rand Paul says he plans to send a criminal contempt referral directly to the Department of Justice after Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment.
story: Senators discuss what could come next as the contempt vote against former White House COVID adviser Anthony Fauci is underway, sharing possibilities of a court battle and procedural hurdles ahead. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Republican senators debated Sen. Rand Paul's, R-Ky., plan to send a criminal contempt referral against former White House COVID advisor Anthony Fauci directly to the Department of Justice, raising questions about the legal viability of the effort and the procedural path forward.

Paul, the leader of the push, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that he was confident the votes would be there to move forward with holding Fauci in contempt of Congress, and that his next plan is to move forward with sending the referral directly over to the Justice Department.
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said his office has already begun drafting a memo to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to urge the Justice Department to pursue a criminal contempt case against Fauci.
RAND PAUL PREDICTS FAUCI CONTEMPT VOTE WILL PASS, VOWS SWIFT DOJ REFERRAL

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., says his office is drafting a memo to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to urge the Justice Department to pursue a criminal contempt case against Anthony Fauci. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"My team is working right now on a memo to Blanche explaining why we think that he can be prosecuted for contempt of Congress," Hawley told Fox News Digital. "He's not entitled to immunity, taken the Fifth, when he already has a pardon. It’s one or the other. "
After the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted Thursday to hold Fauci in contempt, the next step is typically for a full Senate vote to be held.
"It's got to actually go through the full Senate," said Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla. "That's the challenge."

But Paul’s more unusual plan to skip the vote in the Senate and send the criminal referral straight to the Justice Department could be a viable route. Vice President J.D. Vance, the President of the Senate, would have to certify the resolution and refer it to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia. This could make it easier to prosecute Fauci as it wouldn’t require 60 votes in the Senate.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: WHY FAUCI'S 111 FIFTH AMENDMENT PLEAS COULD END UP BEFORE THE COURTS
Vice President JD Vance attends a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland on July 31, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)
Lankford said the risk in utilizing this procedure would be Democrats' potential use of it to their advantage in the future.

"The vice president would have to make a decision if he wants to try to change the structure of what has been done in the Senate, because then that would make them vulnerable three years from now to a future, maybe, Democrat Senate," Lankford said.
Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., backed Paul’s decision to send the contempt referral to the Justice Department, as she believes it is "necessary" to be resolved in a court regardless.

"I think Rand Paul feels very strongly that you can't have him coming in and pleading the Fifth in this situation," Moody said. "I think he also believes ultimately this will wind up in a court and that will be clarified by a court, and I think that's probably necessary as we move forward."
CAN FAUCI HIDE BEHIND THE FIFTH? GAME-CHANGING BIDEN PARDON MAY NOT PROVIDE COMPLETE COVER, EXPERTS SAY

Fauci is under a presidential pardon for all actions taken between Jan. 1, 2014, and Jan. 19, 2025, from former President Joe Biden, which has prompted widespread doubt on whether he is able to invoke his Fifth Amendment right to not self-incriminate.

Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital he questions whether there is a sufficient legal basis for holding Fauci in contempt, arguing that his invocation of the Fifth Amendment complicates the case.

"The first thing you have to do is identify what it is that you would be holding him in contempt for," Rounds said. "I think he took the Fifth. And doing so, I think it makes it more difficult for anybody to actually suggest that."
He also urged his colleagues to remember the fear they all shared during that time period, over the rapidly increasing death rate and the looming uncertainty.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Whether the advice was really good advice or if it was the best advice they had, it was a different time period," Rounds said. "So I just hope we all remember that."
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Trump says US has 'massive' munitions stockpile, vows 'treasonous' leakers being hunted down
summary: Trump says the U.S. has a "massive" munitions stockpile and vows "treasonous" leakers will face long jail sentences after reports of depleted weapons.
story: President Donald Trump signals a potential diplomatic breakthrough with Iran, declaring his preference for a deal over conflict. Fox News' Trey Yingst reports the latest on the conflict from Tel Aviv and Hudson Institute senior fellow Rebeccah Heinrichs also joined 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the latest on the effort to secure a deal.

President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the U.S. has a "massive" munitions stockpile and "treasonous" leakers are "being hunted down" after reports emerged claiming the U.S. Army has burned through nearly all of its stockpiles of two of its primary long-range precision weapons.

The Army has used "virtually all" of its inventories of Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) during the five-month conflict with Iran, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with internal U.S. military data.

"The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types. Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history," Trump wrote on Truth Social early Thursday.
"The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!" the president added.
ALARMING MISSILE REPORT DRAWS FORCEFUL RESPONSE FROM TRUMP AS IRAN WAR TESTS AMERICA’S ARSENAL
President Donald Trump arrives at an event at the Red Rock Resort in Las Vegas on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP)
Trump’s message was reposted on X by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
If accurate, the Reuters report underscores a long-standing Pentagon concern: America's most sophisticated precision weapons can be expended in months but often take years to replace.
Officials fear the drawdown could complicate the military's ability to respond to future crises involving adversaries such as China and Russia, according to the report.
WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST
A MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile (SAM) system on display, Aug. 15, 2019, at Katterbach Army Airfield in Ansbach, Germany. (U.S. Army photo by Charles Rosemond)

Reuters also reported that the conflict significantly reduced inventories of Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors, along with Tomahawk cruise missiles, though the Pentagon has maintained the U.S. military retains the capabilities needed to carry out operations worldwide.
Exact U.S. weapons stockpile figures remain classified for national security reasons.

Some estimates show the U.S. has used more than half of its stockpiles of some weapons systems in the war with Iran. The Center for Strategic and International Studies found the U.S. has enough missiles to continue fighting in Iran under any plausible scenario, but the group says the true issue with the shrinking stockpiles is future wars.

"The depletion of munitions was a major topic and a major reason for the suspension of air attacks," Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marine colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department, told Fox News' Bret Baier. "Our inventories were getting way below what the war planners wanted. That might encourage China to do something."
CSIS notes many munition stockpiles are substantial but focused its analysis on seven key weapons that have been effective in Iran and would also be valuable in a possible Pacific conflict.

title: Sanders' answer when asked if he will endorse socialist Hong in Wisconsin sparks instant mockery: 'Says a lot'
summary: Bernie Sanders says he won't endorse DSA member Francesca Hong's Wisconsin governor bid, sparking mockery given his support for other candidates.
story: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday on the Pod Save America podcast that he doesn't think he'll endorse Wisconsin Democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong. (Credit: YouTube/Pod Save America - Aug. 5)

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., was asked if he would endorse Democratic Socialist of America (DSA) member Francesca Hong’s Wisconsin gubernatorial bid, and his response sparked immediate mockery on social media.

"I don’t think so," the Vermont socialist told "Pod Save America" host Jon Favreau when asked if he is going to endorse Hong’s campaign for governor. "I met Francesca a couple of years ago. I was in Wisconsin, and she seems very, very nice, but again this is a race I’m just not that familiar with."

Sanders added that "we have not gotten involved in many governors' races" other than recently in Maine, where he endorsed Democrat Troy Jackson, who ultimately replaced disgraced Senate candidate Graham Platner, a candidate Sanders endorsed.

Political commentators quickly chimed in on social media suggesting that Sanders not endorsing Hong shows the senator doesn’t think she can win, with many pointing to Sanders’ strident support of Platner despite all of his political baggage.
AFTER PLATNER IMPLOSION, MAINE DEMOCRATS RUSH TOWARD NEW SENATE NOMINEE DESPITE FRESH WARNING SIGNS
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday on the Pod Save America podcast that he doesn't think he'll endorse Democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong. (Fox News)

"Bernie says he’s not backing Francesca Hong because he’s focused on the Senate," Washington Free Beacon reporter Chuck Ross posted on X. "Yet he’s endorsed in mayoral races, House races, and Troy Jackson’s failed governor race in Maine. That’s how whacky Hong is".
"Says a lot," Politico reporter Will Steakin posted on X.
"Guy with the Nazi Tattoo ‘hey everyone makes mistakes’," conservative commentator Stephen L. Miller posted on X. "Crazy communist lady - ‘not my cup of tea sorry.’"
SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong listens to Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speak before being introduced during a campaign rally on Aug. 2, 2026, in Milwaukee. Hong, a democratic socialist in the state legislature, has seen an uptick in recent poll numbers. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images)

"This guy endorsed a guy with a natzi [sic] tat but thinks @FrancescaHongWi is not worth an endorsement……," Jerry Ponio, legislative director for Americans for Prosperity - Wisconsin, posted on X. "Yikes."
"Well, I guess even Bernie enjoys celebrating Thanksgiving at one of his three houses," an account ran by Hong’s likely general election opponent, Republican Tom Tiffany, posted on X.
Tiffany’s post references a controversial quote from Hong that went viral on social media where she suggested canceling Thanksgiving.
"Francesca Hong, who is a Socialist candidate for Governor of Wisconsin is too radical...even for Bernie Sanders," Turning Point Action Northeast Manager Brandon Maly posted on X.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Hong campaign and Sanders’ office for comment.

Critics have argued that Francesca Hong's politics are too far to the left for a swing state like Wisconsin, contending that her identification as a socialist and support for ambitious progressive policies could make her less competitive in a general election.
Hong’s social media account is littered with far-left pledges like abolishing the U.S. Senate and defunding the police.

Sen. Bernie Sanders reacts to questions from a Fox News Digital reporter about Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner’s resurfaced Reddit posts while walking through the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Hong recently tried to walk back those positions in recent interviews ahead of Tuesday’s gubernatorial primary against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, former Wisconsin Department of Administration secretary Joel Brennan, and Democratic state Sen. Kelda Roys.
Polls suggest Hong is likely to comfortably win that contest, which will advance her to a race against Tiffany, the likely Republican nominee, in November.

title: Your blood pressure cuff may expose your health data
summary: FTC cases reveal major health apps disclosed blood pressure and glucose data to advertising and analytics companies without users realizing it.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Every morning, you strap on the cuff, press the button and watch the number pop up on your phone. It feels private. It feels like it is just between you and your app. That sense of privacy can be misleading.

Depending on the app and your settings, that reading, along with your glucose numbers, weight and medication schedule, may be stored in the cloud or shared with service providers. FTC cases show that some health apps have also disclosed sensitive information to advertising and analytics companies. Separately, data brokers market health-related profiles that scammers could exploit.
Here's what may be happening behind the screen of your health app and how to limit the exposure.
