ARE INSURANCE APPS WATCHING YOU?
A home blood pressure monitor can send sensitive health readings to a connected app, where privacy protections may vary. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The app on your phone isn't your doctor's office
Here's the assumption almost everyone makes: "My health data is protected. Isn't that what HIPAA is for?" Often, no.

HIPAA generally protects health information held by covered healthcare providers, health plans and their business associates. A consumer app you choose independently often falls outside HIPAA. However, an app may come under HIPAA when it handles protected health information on behalf of a covered provider or health plan.

Apps outside HIPAA do not operate without any rules. Many may still fall under the FTC's Health Breach Notification Rule, state consumer health laws and general protections against unfair or deceptive business practices.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., introduced the Health Information Privacy Reform Act. The proposal would extend HIPAA-like privacy, security and breach-notification standards to some health information held outside the traditional HIPAA system. It would also require plain-language warnings before certain technologies begin generating wellness data that HIPAA does not protect.
As of today, the proposal remains introduced and has not become law. That means the same blood sugar reading can receive different legal protections depending on who holds it and why.
What these apps are actually doing with your data
You would think a company that builds a blood pressure app would only use your numbers to track your blood pressure. Federal regulators have repeatedly found otherwise.

GoodRx agreed to pay a $1.5 million civil penalty to settle FTC allegations that it failed to report unauthorized disclosures of health information to Facebook, Google and other companies. The FTC said GoodRx uploaded identifiers connected to people who had purchased certain heart disease and blood pressure medications so Facebook could target them with ads.BetterHelp agreed to pay $7.8 million after the FTC alleged that it shared email addresses, IP addresses and answers to personal health questions with Facebook, Snapchat, Pinterest and Criteo for advertising. About 800,000 people later received notices that they were eligible for refunds.Flo Health settled FTC allegations that it shared sensitive health data from millions of users with Facebook, Google and other analytics providers. In a separate class action, Flo agreed to contribute $8 million toward settlements totaling $59.5 million. Google agreed to pay $48 million, and Flurry agreed to pay $3.5 million.Premom's developer agreed to pay a total of $200,000 to resolve federal and state allegations involving its privacy practices. The FTC alleged that the fertility app disclosed sensitive health and location information to Google and two China-based analytics companies.

GoodRx agreed to pay a $1.5 million civil penalty to settle FTC allegations that it failed to report unauthorized disclosures of health information to Facebook, Google and other companies. The FTC said GoodRx uploaded identifiers connected to people who had purchased certain heart disease and blood pressure medications so Facebook could target them with ads.

BetterHelp agreed to pay $7.8 million after the FTC alleged that it shared email addresses, IP addresses and answers to personal health questions with Facebook, Snapchat, Pinterest and Criteo for advertising. About 800,000 people later received notices that they were eligible for refunds.

Flo Health settled FTC allegations that it shared sensitive health data from millions of users with Facebook, Google and other analytics providers. In a separate class action, Flo agreed to contribute $8 million toward settlements totaling $59.5 million. Google agreed to pay $48 million, and Flurry agreed to pay $3.5 million.

Premom's developer agreed to pay a total of $200,000 to resolve federal and state allegations involving its privacy practices. The FTC alleged that the fertility app disclosed sensitive health and location information to Google and two China-based analytics companies.

These were not obscure apps built by scammers. They were mainstream health services, and regulators alleged that the sharing happened through ordinary advertising and analytics tools running in the background.

That does not mean every blood pressure app behaves the same way. However, it gives you a strong reason to check what your own app collects, where it stores the information and which companies receive it.
ARE APPLE DEVICES SPYING? WHAT YOUR IPHONE TRACKS
Digital blood pressure systems make tracking easier, but they can also create another path for health data to leave your control. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The data broker connection: Your condition has a price tag

Here's the part that should genuinely unsettle you. A Duke University researcher contacted 37 data brokers as a prospective buyer. Twenty-six responded, and 11 were willing and able to sell mental health data. Some advertised information tied to depression, anxiety and other conditions, along with demographic details. One broker advertised names and postal addresses connected to specific conditions. Prices ranged from $275 for aggregated counts to annual licensing fees of $75,000 or more.

This problem reaches beyond mental health, as data brokers can collect and sell many forms of health-related information. The FTC has documented data broker categories related to pregnancy, diabetes, high cholesterol and other potentially sensitive health interests.

In a final order issued in December 2025, California's privacy regulator fined Datamasters $45,000 for failing to register as a data broker. The order said the company bought and resold contact lists tied to sensitive conditions.

Those lists included 435,245 postal addresses associated with Alzheimer's disease, more than 2.3 million associated with blindness or visual impairment, 133,142 associated with addiction and 857,449 associated with bladder-control issues. California's enforcement chief warned that reselling lists connected to Alzheimer's disease could enable targeting that goes far beyond ordinary advertising.

If you want to look up your exposed information online, now is the time. Get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web and show how vulnerable you might be: CyberGuy.com.
How scammers use a 'medically profiled' list

Put yourself in a scammer's shoes for a second. Random cold-calling is a numbers game. Most people hang up. However, a list of people associated with diabetes or high blood pressure could help a scammer choose a much more convincing lie, including fake Medicare and healthcare offers.

A caller claims to be from Medicare or a diabetes association and offers free glucose meters or test strips. All they need is your Medicare number "to process the shipment." Federal health officials have warned about callers impersonating Medicare, Social Security or diabetes organizations while offering free glucose meters, test strips and other supplies. The supplies may never arrive, or someone may fraudulently bill Medicare using your information.

A caller could reference your blood pressure or diabetes like a nurse checking in, then pivot to a plan that supposedly covers exactly what you need. Knowing a real detail about your health does not prove the caller represents Medicare, your doctor or an insurance company.

Ads, emails or calls may push treatments or supplements connected to a condition associated with your profile. Their timing may make the offer feel personal, but that does not make the medical claim or the seller legitimate. A scammer does not need to hack your phone to personalize a pitch. Health-related information can come from commercial profiles, public records, online activity, data breaches or other sources. A medically segmented list could help a caller make a fraudulent offer sound far more believable.

You do not have to. That is what makes this so hard to see coming. Your blood pressure app, glucose monitor and smart scale can each add information to a larger profile, depending on the service, its partners and the settings you enable. Data brokers may also compile property records, voter files, online activity and information purchased from other companies. Once information enters this ecosystem, companies may buy, resell, combine and refresh it across data broker and people-search services you have never heard of.
The cuff may look simple, but the information it collects can reveal personal details about your health and medical conditions. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How exposed is your specific device?

Not every app behaves the same way. Some provide stronger privacy controls than others. Features, settings and company practices can change, so review the current privacy notices for every service you use.

Connected OMRON monitors can transfer readings to the OMRON Connect app through Bluetooth, where you can upload, store and share your heart health history. Data handling may depend on your device, permissions and connected services, so review OMRON's current privacy notices before syncing.

Certain Dexcom products fall under HIPAA when Dexcom or a healthcare provider supplies them as insurance-reimbursable products in the United States. Other Dexcom websites, support programs and services may process information outside that HIPAA-covered context. Dexcom also provides opt-outs for certain data sales, sharing and targeted advertising under applicable state laws.

Withings says it does not share health information with advertising partners. It may share some non-health personal information to deliver tailored advertising, and information can sync with outside apps or partners when you authorize a connection.

Google committed not to use health and wellness information collected from Fitbit devices for Google Ads and to keep that information in a separate data silo. That commitment came through regulatory conditions attached to Google's Fitbit acquisition, so continue reviewing current Fitbit and Google privacy controls.

If you choose pharmacy or coupon features, Medisafe says your personal information may be disclosed to partner pharmacies or coupon companies. Those companies will then handle the information under their own privacy practices.

Your device encrypts Health information, and iCloud uses end-to-end encryption when you enable the required account protections. In addition, Apple prohibits apps from using HealthKit data for advertising. You decide which outside apps can read or write individual categories of Health information.
The takeaway is that you have more control than you might think, but you need to go into the settings and use it.
Lock it down: Your 20-minute privacy tune-up
Here's a simple step-by-step guide to increasing your privacy when using health apps.
iPhone: Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Tracking, then turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track. Next, go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Apple Advertising and turn off Personalized Ads.

Android: Go to Settings > Google > All services > Ads > Ads privacy. From there, you can turn off ad topics, app-suggested ads and ad measurement. Some devices also provide an option to delete the advertising ID. Menu names can vary by phone.

These settings limit certain forms of advertising and cross-app tracking. They do not stop every app from collecting information you enter directly or using other identifiers allowed under its privacy policy.
Open the account or privacy settings in each health app you use. Switch off anything labeled marketing, ad personalization or third-party sharing. Disconnect any linked apps you do not actively use.

Check for links labeled "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information," "Your Privacy Choices" or something similar. Covered businesses must provide these controls under laws such as California's CCPA when they sell or share personal information as the law defines those terms. Your available rights may depend on where you live. An opt-out can restrict certain data practices, but it does not guarantee that all of your information will remain with the company.

Medicare does not make unsolicited calls offering free medical supplies in exchange for your Medicare or financial information. If a caller references a specific health condition, the detail may have come from a commercial profile, public record, data breach or another source. Do not assume the caller is legitimate simply because they know something about you. Never confirm personal or Medicare information during an unexpected call.

Turning off tracking in your apps can help reduce future collection, but it does not remove information that companies have already gathered, shared or sold. That data may already appear across dozens or even hundreds of broker and people-search sites.
You can submit removal requests yourself, but the process takes time. Each site has its own opt-out steps, and you may need to repeat them because your information can reappear months later.

A reputable data removal service can handle much of that work for you. These services send opt-out requests to data brokers, monitor for reappearing information and submit new removal requests when needed.
No service can erase every trace of your information online, but ongoing removal can reduce how much personal data is available to advertisers, scammers and identity thieves.

Kurt's key takeaways

Your health app may not receive the same HIPAA protections as your doctor's office. FTC cases show that some major health platforms disclosed sensitive information to advertising and analytics companies, while data brokers market profiles connected to health conditions. Scammers could use details like these to make Medicare, pharmacy and supplement pitches sound more believable. Turn off tracking and sharing where possible, and use available deletion or opt-out requests for information companies have already collected.

title: One-wheeled AI security robot could patrol your property
summary: The 1Rollo one-wheeled AI security robot uses a spinning flywheel to balance while patrolling properties at speeds up to 19 mph on a single charge.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

What if the next security guard rolling past your office had one wheel and never needed a coffee break? That is the pitch behind 1Rollo, a one-wheeled AI security robot from Estonian startup Rollo Robotics. The company believes its narrow design could patrol large properties at a lower operating cost than traditional security vehicles.

The machine follows mapped routes while watching the area around it. When its artificial intelligence detects unusual activity, 1Rollo can alert a human operator. That person can review the situation and decide whether to send a security guard.

For now, 1Rollo remains a functional prototype. Rollo Robotics says it plans to make the robot commercially available in 2027. Therefore, its design and specifications could change before customers begin using it.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
HUMANOID ROBOT SKIN SENSES PEOPLE BEFORE CONTACT
The 1Rollo uses a self-balancing single-wheel design to patrol outdoor properties autonomously. (Rollo Robotics)
How the 1Rollo AI security robot patrols property

1Rollo uses a 360-degree computer vision system to monitor its surroundings. It also relies on Real-Time Kinematic Global Navigation Satellite System positioning (RTK GNSS). RTK uses correction data to provide more precise positioning than standard satellite navigation. That precision could help the robot stay close to its assigned route around a business or industrial property. As the robot moves, its cameras and sensors look for obstacles. The system can then adjust its path to avoid a collision. Meanwhile, the AI analyzes the area for anomalies. If the system spots something unusual, it can send an alert over Wi-Fi or a 4G or 5G connection.
How the one-wheeled security robot stays balanced

Keeping a 100-pound robot upright on one wheel takes more than a clever-looking design. Rollo Robotics uses a vertically positioned spinning flywheel inside the machine. The flywheel sits in line with the main wheel and helps the robot maintain its balance. To turn, the system tilts the internal flywheel toward either side. Rollo Robotics describes the hardware and software behind this method as patent-pending. The single-wheel design gives the robot a narrow footprint. As a result, it may travel through spaces where a wider patrol vehicle would struggle. However, Rollo Robotics has not published detailed performance results for stairs, steep slopes or deeply uneven ground. Those real-world tests will show where the monowheel design works best.
1Rollo security robot speed and battery life

The company's current specifications list 1Rollo at about 43 inches tall. Its wheel measures 24 inches across, while the complete robot weighs approximately 100 pounds. Rollo Robotics lists a top speed of 19 mph. That is much faster than the walking pace of many existing security robots. Battery life reaches up to eight hours per charge, according to the company. The product information also lists autonomous wireless charging.
FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS
The 1Rollo can follow predefined patrol routes while its cameras and sensors monitor the surrounding area. (Rollo Robotics)
How cameras and sensors expand 1Rollo patrols

The standard robot includes a 360-degree vision system. However, Rollo Robotics designed the platform to support additional equipment. Customers could add thermal cameras for low-light environments. The platform can also support pan-tilt-zoom cameras for viewing activity farther away. Other compatible equipment includes night vision, RFID systems and custom payloads. These options could help companies adapt the robot for a specific property.
How operators could manage a 1Rollo robot fleet

A cloud-based management platform would allow operators to monitor multiple robots from one location. Security teams could define patrol routes and review performance through the platform. An operator could also watch a live feed after receiving an alert. The robot includes a microphone and speaker. Therefore, the operator could speak with someone near the machine without immediately sending a guard. We have seen a similar approach with the Ascento Guard autonomous security robot. That machine also patrols property while human operators handle serious incidents.

However, robots still need to prove they provide meaningful results. Dublin, Ohio, recently retired an AI robot cop that recorded no arrests during its parking garage pilot. That case does not predict how 1Rollo will perform. Still, it shows why customers should establish clear goals before deploying autonomous security technology.
How the 1Rollo subscription model could work

Rollo Robotics plans to offer 1Rollo through a Robotics-as-a-Service model. Customers would subscribe to the service instead of buying the robot outright. According to CEO and co-founder Sander Sebastian Agur, the subscription would include access to current hardware, software updates and support. The model could remove a large upfront equipment expense. It may also make repairs and future upgrades easier for customers. Rollo Robotics says its goal is to reduce operating costs compared with relying on human guards or patrol vehicles. However, the company has not announced subscription pricing.
Rollo Robotics designed the 1Rollo to patrol campuses, industrial sites and other large outdoor properties. (Rollo Robotics)
AI security robot privacy and cybersecurity questions

A connected robot may improve physical security while creating new digital concerns. 1Rollo uses wireless connections and a cloud platform. Therefore, customers should ask how the company encrypts camera feeds and protects operator accounts. They should also ask where recordings are stored. Clear deletion policies will become important for employees and visitors who appear on camera. Meanwhile, the robot needs a safe way to handle a lost internet connection. It should keep avoiding people and obstacles even when a remote operator cannot reach it. Buyers should also learn how Rollo Robotics delivers security updates. A compromised patrol robot could expose video or provide unauthorized access to its controls. Lawmakers have already raised similar concerns about autonomous machines. A proposed federal bill would restrict government use of some foreign robots over national security fears. Rollo Robotics operates in Estonia, but every connected robot deserves the same cybersecurity review.
What this means to you

You probably will not find a one-wheeled robot guarding people's driveway anytime soon. However, businesses could begin seeing machines like 1Rollo around warehouses or office campuses. Large private properties may also use them to cover areas that guards cannot watch continuously. The robot could handle repetitive patrols while people make decisions during an incident. That may also keep guards away from hazardous areas until they understand what is happening. Still, a moving camera can feel more intrusive than one mounted on a wall. Employees and visitors deserve to know when the robot records them. They should also know who can watch the footage and how long the company keeps it. Those answers should arrive before the robot begins its first patrol.
Kurt's key takeaways

1Rollo looks unusual, but the idea behind it makes sense. A narrow autonomous machine could cover large properties without the bulk of a security vehicle. The human operator also remains part of the process. The robot detects activity and sends an alert, while a person decides what should happen next. However, the polished demonstration is only the beginning. Rollo Robotics still needs to show that 1Rollo can handle changing weather, crowded spaces and long shifts without constant assistance. Pricing will play a major role too. Businesses need to know whether the subscription saves money and delivers better security than existing systems.

title: DoorDash gets FAA approval for its own delivery drones
summary: DoorDash earned FAA Part 135 air carrier certification and launched DoorDash Air, but several operational approvals remain before drones reach customers.
story: FOX Business correspondent Madison Alworth reports on drone food delivery services launching in New Jersey on ‘America Reports.’

Your next DoorDash order could arrive with a flight path instead of a driver. DoorDash has earned FAA Part 135 air carrier certification and launched DoorDash Air, its in-house drone delivery program. The company now has federal authorization to operate a commercial drone delivery service in the United States.

Yes, the app you use for burgers, groceries and late-night snacks is entering the airline business. However, this does not mean a DoorDash drone will hover over your driveway tomorrow. The company still needs added operational approvals. It also has not announced its first markets or a firm launch schedule for its custom aircraft.

AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE
DoorDash Air plans to use company-built drones to deliver eligible food, medicine and everyday essentials. (DoorDash)
DoorDash becomes a certified air carrier

DoorDash announced the FAA certification on July 29, 2026. The company says it is the eighth drone operator to earn this type of federal air carrier certificate. The FAA uses Part 135 certification for companies that carry other people's property for payment. For drones, it provides the regulatory path for commercial package deliveries beyond a pilot's direct line of sight.

Getting certified requires a five-phase FAA review. The agency evaluates the operator's aircraft, maintenance procedures and safety program. Even after earning the certificate, an operator still needs airspace authorization. It may also need exemptions or waivers for flights beyond visual line of sight. State rules and local land-use requirements can also affect where a delivery hub operates. So, DoorDash has cleared a major federal hurdle. Still, each real-world delivery network will require more planning and approval.
Why DoorDash wants to deliver orders by drone

Anyone who has watched a hot meal slowly travel across town can understand the appeal. DoorDash says more than 20% of its orders in 2025 traveled between three and five miles. Those orders took nearly 25% longer than shorter trips, according to the company.

DoorDash blames part of that delay on the challenge of matching a Dasher with a mid-range order. A driver may prefer several shorter deliveries near a busy restaurant area instead of one longer trip. A drone could take the longer order while a Dasher remains close to restaurants. As a result, the customer could get a faster delivery while the driver moves on to another nearby order.

DoorDash estimates that drone deliveries completed during 2025 took an average of about 25 minutes. The company also says some locations in its partner drone pilots saw order volume rise by roughly 30%. That increase continued during the nine weeks after the pilot began. Those are DoorDash's figures, so performance could change by location, weather and the type of order. Still, they help explain why the company wants more control over the aircraft carrying its deliveries.
CHINESE DRONE MONOPOLY PUT ON NOTICE AMID CONCERNS OVER CCP SPYING: 'STRATEGIC MISTAKE'
DoorDash will continue its partnerships with drone partners like Alphabet's Wing as it designs its own aircraft. (DoorDash)
DoorDash Air will build its own delivery drones
That is the same robotics and autonomy group behind DoorDash's Dot delivery robot.

DoorDash says its drone will be designed and built in the United States. The majority of its components will also come from the U.S., according to the company. DoorDash has not revealed the aircraft's range, payload capacity or final design. A DoorDash spokesperson told CyberGuy that the company plans to share more details about those specifics this fall.
DoorDash drones will work alongside human Dashers

DoorDash says Dashers will continue handling the vast majority of its daily deliveries. That makes sense. A drone cannot walk into an apartment building or carry a large catering order upstairs. It also may struggle with bad weather or a location without a suitable drop zone.
Instead, DoorDash wants its Autonomous Delivery Platform to select the best method for each order. The platform can assign a Dasher. It can also choose an autonomous option such as Dot or a drone.

For example, a small order traveling four miles to a suburban house may fit a drone. A large grocery order going to a high-rise apartment will likely need a person. This approach follows a broader shift across the delivery industry. Uber Eats has also moved toward drone deliveries, while other companies continue testing robots and airborne delivery systems.
What the FAA certification does not guarantee

FAA certification gives DoorDash the legal foundation to operate an air carrier. It does not provide blanket permission to begin unlimited drone flights in every city. DoorDash has not announced its first DoorDash Air markets. The company also has not provided a detailed timeline for deliveries using its in-house aircraft.

In addition, longer autonomous routes may require FAA approval for beyond visual line of sight operations. Local zoning, environmental reviews and community concerns can also shape where hubs are built. Noise could become a major issue. The FAA notes that drone noise may bother a community even when it falls below the level of a significant environmental impact.
Therefore, early service will likely remain limited to carefully selected areas. Suburban neighborhoods with predictable routes and open drop-off spaces may prove easier than dense urban blocks.
JETBLUE FLIGHT REPORTS DRONE STRIKE DURING APPROACH TO NEW YORK AIRPORT: FAA
DoorDash says drones will handle select orders while human Dashers continue making most of the company’s deliveries. (DoorDash)
What this means to you

DoorDash drone delivery could shorten the wait for small, urgent orders. Cold medicine could arrive without waiting for a driver to cross town. A nurse finishing a long shift might get a hot meal faster. A forgotten phone charger could reach you before your battery runs out. However, availability will depend heavily on where you live. Your address may need to fall within an eligible drone delivery zone. The order must also meet the aircraft's weight and size limits. DoorDash told CyberGuy that it is testing the aircraft to operate across a wider range of weather conditions and climates. The company said it will pause operations during extreme weather until conditions return to an operable level.

You should also look closely at the final cost. DoorDash has not said whether its new in-house DoorDash Air service will carry a separate fee or change how tipping works. The company also has not explained whether customers will choose between a DoorDash Air drone and a Dasher once the new service launches. DoorDash's current partner-operated program does allow eligible customers to select drone delivery at checkout.

For now, think of DoorDash Air as an important step toward wider service rather than a nationwide launch. The federal certificate gives DoorDash the regulatory foundation to operate its own commercial drone delivery service. However, individual operations may still require airspace authorization and other FAA approvals. The next test will be whether DoorDash can make drone delivery reliable enough for an ordinary Tuesday night dinner. For more background on how companies are already testing airborne orders, check out how drones are changing food delivery.
Kurt's key takeaways

DoorDash has spent years learning how to move orders through streets. Now it wants to control what happens in the sky. FAA certification gives DoorDash Air a serious start. The company has the app, the restaurant relationships and billions of past orders to study. It also knows where deliveries slow down. Still, building a drone is only one piece of the job. DoorDash must prove that its aircraft can operate safely and consistently. It must also keep food intact while avoiding noise problems and neighborhood resistance. Human Dashers are not disappearing. Instead, DoorDash wants drones and robots to handle specific trips that could be faster without a car.

Would you trust a DoorDash drone to lower dinner into your yard, or would the sound of delivery aircraft flying over your neighborhood ruin the convenience? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake party invitation scam can hijack your computer
summary: Fake party invitations trick victims into downloading malware that gives criminals remote access to computers and spreads through contact lists.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

You sit down at your computer to clear out your inbox. Then you spot a party invitation from someone you recognize. Maybe it appears to come from a friend. Perhaps the sender belongs to a group you know. Either way, the familiar name makes the message feel safe enough to open.

Inside, everything looks cheerful. There is an envelope graphic, a friendly note and what appears to be an invitation for a wedding or retirement party. However, you cannot see the event details yet. The message tells you to save the invitation or install something to join the guest list.

That request should stop you cold. A legitimate party invitation should not require you to install software before you can see when or where the event takes place. That small download could give a criminal remote access to your computer. Here’s how this fake invitation scam works and what you can do before one click puts your computer and contacts at risk.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA
A fake party invitation can trick recipients into downloading software that gives criminals remote access to a Windows computer. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How malicious party invitations reach your inbox

The scam begins with trust. An invitation appears to come from someone whose name you recognize, so you become less suspicious. Criminals may copy the look of a legitimate invitation platform. They can add a colorful envelope, an exclusive-sounding message and a button that promises to reveal the details.

The email has one main purpose: getting you to click. Once you press the invitation, the message sends you to a separate website. That page says a friend sent you something and asks you to download a file to view it.
The request may seem simple. Still, party invitations normally open inside a website or app. They do not need to install a program on your computer.
Why the fake invitation page looks convincing

The landing page may contain a large "Download invitation" button. It may also display a familiar company name inside the web address. However, seeing a trusted brand somewhere in a link proves very little. Criminals can place that name inside a much longer address or add extra letters that make the domain look authentic at a glance.

You need to identify the real domain instead of focusing on the first familiar word you see. The page may also create confusion. It could claim that your invitation is already downloading while another message asks you to click if the download fails. Some versions even include a testimonial from a supposed guest who says opening the invitation was easy.

A review on a private party invitation page should feel strange. Those details are designed to quiet your doubts and push you toward the download button. For more visual breakdowns of scams like this, check out The CyberGuy Report podcast at CyberGuy.com.
What happens after you download the fake invitation

In the example we describe, the website directs you to open the file on a Windows computer. That device-specific request is another major warning sign. Why would a party invitation care which device you use? The malicious file may contain a remote access tool. Businesses use legitimate versions of this software to troubleshoot computers from another location.

Criminals can abuse similar tools to control your system without permission. Once you install the file, an attacker may be able to search your computer or access saved information. The exact damage depends on the program and the permissions it receives. Your email account can become an especially valuable target. It contains personal conversations along with a contact list filled with people who trust you.

The criminals can then send the same fake invitation to your friends and relatives. Those people may open it because the message appears to come from your real account. As a result, one compromised computer can start a chain reaction.
Why these invitation scams keep working

People receive a steady stream of spam, fake alerts and impersonation attempts. Criminals can also use AI tools to create cleaner writing and more realistic designs. That makes the familiar sender name even more powerful.

You may be cautious around a message from a stranger. Yet you might act quickly when the invitation appears to come from someone you know. The scam succeeds when familiarity replaces verification. Email providers and technology companies continue to improve their filters. Even so, dangerous messages still reach real inboxes. That leaves you making the final decision about whether a link deserves your trust.
HOTEL WI-FI PHISHING ATTACK TARGETS MICROSOFT LOGINS
Scam emails may appear to come from a trusted contact and use cheerful invitation graphics to make a malicious download seem legitimate. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to stay safe from fake party invitation scams
A few precautions can help you recognize a malicious invitation before it compromises your computer or accounts.

Use strong antivirus software and keep it actively running in the background on your devices. Real-time protection can warn you about a dangerous link or block a malicious download before it reaches your computer.

If you clicked the invitation or downloaded a suspicious file, delete the file without opening it and run a full security scan. A scan can help identify unwanted software that may have reached your computer. Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated as well. Updates often close weaknesses that criminals try to exploit. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

Stop immediately if an invitation tells you to download or install a program before you can see the event. Real invitation services normally show the details in your browser or inside their official app. You should not need a separate installer. Delete the message instead of trying to see what happens next.

On a computer, place your cursor over a link without pressing it. Your browser or email program should reveal the destination address. Read the entire address carefully. Watch for misspellings, unexpected words or extra letters added around a legitimate company name. A familiar logo does not confirm that the link belongs to the real company.

Avoid using the link inside the email when you have doubts. Instead, type the invitation service's web address into your browser or open its official app. Sign in and look for the invitation there. If it does not appear in your account, the email may be fake.

Reach out through a separate text message or phone call if an invitation feels unusual. Do not reply directly to the suspicious email. A criminal may control the sender's account or may have forged the address. Ask whether the person actually sent the invitation and whether it requires a download.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Legitimate digital invitations should not require users to install software before viewing an event’s date, location or guest information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Your risk is generally lower if you visited the page but did not run anything. Close the browser tab without pressing the download button. If the file has already downloaded, leave it closed and delete it. Opening the file gives the malicious program a chance to run. Never open it simply to find out what it contains.

Use your email provider's Report phishing option before deleting the invitation. Reporting the message can help the provider block similar emails and warn other recipients. You can also block the sender if you do not recognize the address.

A data removal service can help remove your details from many public data broker databases. This may make it harder for scammers to find personal information they can use to make a message feel convincing. However, no service can remove every record. It also cannot prevent a criminal from reaching you through a compromised friend's contact list. Still, reducing your public exposure can give scammers less material to work with. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email account. This adds another barrier if criminals steal or guess your password. Never approve an unexpected login request. Also, do not share a security code with anyone who contacts you.

If you typed your email address, password or security code into the fake page, use a clean device to change that password immediately. Change it anywhere else you reused it. Then review the account for unfamiliar activity, new recovery information or settings you did not change. Use a password manager to create and store a strong, unique password for every account so one stolen login cannot unlock several services.

Disconnect the computer from the internet if you ran the installer or noticed unexpected remote activity. Next, run a full security scan. You may also need help from a trusted computer professional to confirm that the remote access software is gone. Use a different, clean device to change important passwords. Start with your email account because criminals may use it to reset passwords for other services. Also, review your email account for unfamiliar forwarding rules or active login sessions. Warn your contacts if suspicious messages may have gone out under your name.
Kurt's key takeaways

A party invitation should give you information, not demand access to your computer. Delete the message if it asks you to install anything before revealing the event. Check the full destination of every link. Then contact the supposed sender separately when something feels unusual. If you downloaded a file but did not open it, delete it and run a security scan. If you ran the file, disconnect the computer and secure your accounts from a clean device. Most importantly, pay attention to that moment when something feels off. A few seconds of doubt can stop a criminal from getting inside your computer. Want to see more? Check out The CyberGuy Report podcast.
Should email providers face tougher requirements to stop malicious invitations before they ever reach your inbox? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: The scam text test: Spot danger before you tap
summary: A simple six-step scam text test helps you spot phishing messages about fake deliveries, toll notices and bank alerts before you click or share anything.
story: Halimah Delaine Prado, Google General Counsel, reveals the rise of AI-powered phishing scams originating from China's 'outsider enterprise.' She explains how these criminals use artificial intelligence to create highly convincing fake websites, impersonating trusted brands like T-Mobile to defraud hundreds of thousands of Americans, causing millions in losses. Prado highlights Google's strategy to combat these evolving threats.

Your phone buzzes. The text reads, "Your package is delayed. Confirm your address here." A little later, it's a text message about an unpaid toll, suspicious bank activity or an account that will be locked unless you act now.

That's how scam texts work. They don't always look wild or obviously fake. They look routine, urgent and easy to deal with in a hurry. The good news: You don't need to memorize every scam. You just need a quick way to test suspicious messages before you tap. Here's the simple scam text test to run before you click, pay or share anything.

The scam text test
If a text asks you to click, pay, verify, sign in or fix a problem, run through these checks first.

Are you actually waiting for that package? Do you use that bank? Did you recently drive on a toll road? If the answer is no, treat the message as suspicious. Even if the answer is yes, don't assume it's real. Scammers rely on coincidence. They send thousands of similar messages knowing that some recipients will be waiting for a package or use the company being impersonated.
Urgency is one of the biggest red flags. Watch for phrases like:
Act nowFinal warningVerify immediatelyAvoid penaltiesAccount suspended

A real company may send an urgent alert, but scammers use pressure to stop you from checking whether the message is legitimate. Take a breath before responding. A few extra minutes spent verifying the message can prevent days or weeks of dealing with a stolen account.

Many scam texts use vague greetings, odd wording, awkward punctuation or slightly incorrect brand names. You might see a message addressed to "Dear customer" instead of your name. It may refer to a package without showing an order number or claim to come from a bank without identifying the account involved. Good grammar doesn't guarantee a message is safe. What scam texts usually look like
Scam texts often fall into a few familiar categories.

These messages claim a package was delayed, an address needs to be corrected or a small shipping fee must be paid. The link may lead to a fake postal or delivery website that collects your card information, password or home address.

These texts claim someone used your card, your account has been locked or you must verify a transaction immediately. The message may include a phone number connecting you to a scammer pretending to work for the bank.

Toll scams claim you owe a small amount and will face a larger penalty if you don't pay immediately. The amount is often low enough to make paying seem easier than investigating. The payment page then steals your financial information.

These messages claim your email, payment app, streaming service or social media account will be suspended. They direct you to a fake login page designed to capture your username and password. These scams work because each message sounds plausible. The goal is to make you react first and think later.

How antivirus software can help

Good habits are your first line of defense, but strong antivirus software can add another layer of protection. Some security tools can warn you about suspicious links, phishing websites and malicious downloads before they put your information at risk.

The one rule to remember
You never have to solve a surprise text from inside the text. Stop, verify independently and only act through official channels. That one habit can help you avoid a huge number of text scams.
Kurt's key takeaways

Scam texts work because they make an everyday problem feel urgent. A package delay, unpaid toll or bank warning can seem believable enough to make you tap without thinking. Don't use the link or phone number in the message. Open the company's official app, type its website yourself or call a number you already trust. Strong antivirus software can help flag some suspicious texts and fake websites, but no security tool catches everything. Taking a few seconds to verify the message can save you from a stolen account or a costly mistake.

title: Water cyberattack hits at least 7 states
summary: CISA warned about exposed programmable logic controllers weeks before hackers targeted dozens of Minnesota water utilities in a coordinated strike.
story: National correspondent Madeleine Rivera reports on the federal investigation into a cyberattack targeting community water systems in Minnesota and at least six other states. Federal agencies including the FBI, CISA, and the EPA warn that Iran-affiliated threat actors are targeting critical infrastructure. The segment outlines the national security implications of these cyber threats on local utility systems.

You probably never think about the computer systems behind your kitchen faucet. You turn the handle and expect clean water. That familiar routine suddenly felt far less certain in Minnesota and six other states.

A coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 community water systems on Sunday, July 26, and Monday, July 27. Minnesota IT Services, known as MNIT, activated the state's cybersecurity response and brought in federal agencies to help investigate.

One water plant temporarily went offline. Meanwhile, other communities reported problems involving automated controls or communications equipment. Workers switched to manual operations or used backup procedures to keep essential services running. Fortunately, state officials reported no active requests for residents to reduce or change their drinking water use.
The FBI has since said that water or wastewater utility companies in seven states have been affected.
"Some of that activity degraded water operations," the bureau said.
This water cyberattack raises an uncomfortable question for towns across America. How many local utilities could keep operating if hackers gained access to the computers controlling their equipment?
INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

A water tower is seen Thursday, July 30, 2026, in Plymouth, Minn. A cyberattack targeted operating technology at more than 30 water systems in Minnesota, including Plymouth's, earlier this week, state officials said. (Ellen Schmidt/AP)
What happened in the Minnesota water cyberattack

The attack targeted operational technology, commonly called OT. These systems control physical equipment such as pumps, valves and treatment machinery. In Braham, city officials initially reported that the water plant had gone offline for an unknown reason. Crews restored the facility within hours and said it was again filtering and treating water as expected.

Officials later blamed the outage on a malicious cyberattack against computerized operating systems. The city relied on water already stored in its tower while crews worked on the problem. Plymouth reported communications problems involving two water towers and several wastewater lift stations. However, officials said water levels and water quality remained unaffected.

South St. Paul also identified a cybersecurity incident involving automated water utility controls. Public Works employees used established contingency procedures to maintain normal water and wastewater operations. Maple Plain publicly confirmed that its water utility technology had also been targeted.

In total, four communities have publicly described specific effects, although MNIT says attackers targeted more than 30 systems statewide. That difference is important. Being targeted does not mean every system suffered a shutdown. However, it shows that someone tried to reach a large number of local utilities within a short period.
Who may be behind the Minnesota water cyberattack

Officials have not announced a definitive attribution. However, a July 30 report from The New York Times says investigators preliminarily believe Iranian hackers were probably responsible. The report cited U.S. and state officials familiar with the investigation, but President Donald Trump said he rejected the suggestion that Iran was behind the breaches.

Those officials cautioned that the assessment could change as investigators collect more technical evidence. They also have not ruled out the possibility that attackers tried to make the activity appear Iranian. Therefore, Iran should be described as the leading preliminary suspicion rather than the confirmed attacker.

The timing has drawn attention because CISA warned in April that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting internet-exposed programmable logic controllers. These devices help control machinery and other equipment at water systems and additional critical infrastructure facilities. CISA initially highlighted certain Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley controllers. On July 22, the agency expanded its warning to include equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens and potentially other manufacturers.

Still, federal officials have not publicly tied that campaign to the Minnesota incidents. CyberGuy has previously examined Iran's expanding cyber threat to U.S. critical infrastructure. Water systems remain attractive targets because even a limited disruption can create fear far beyond the equipment involved.
IRAN-LINKED HACKERS TARGET US MEDICAL TECH COMPANY
A coordinated cyberattack reached operational technology at dozens of Minnesota water systems, exposing security risks for smaller utilities nationwide. (City of St. Cloud)
Why water system cyberattacks threaten U.S. communities

Minnesota's experience could happen in any state. The United States has close to 170,000 drinking water and wastewater systems. Many now connect physical equipment to internet-enabled technology so workers can monitor facilities from a distance. That remote access helps utilities manage equipment spread across wide service areas. However, it may also give an attacker a route into vital controls when operators fail to secure the connection.

Smaller communities often face the greatest challenge. The Government Accountability Office says water systems have widely different cybersecurity capabilities. Many also use older technology that can be difficult to update. At the same time, utilities must stretch limited budgets across essential repairs and regulatory requirements. Cybersecurity upgrades may compete with work that residents can see, such as replacing aging equipment.

A large utility may employ dedicated security professionals. A small town may rely on plant operators who already handle daily operations and after-hours problems. As a result, the communities with fewer resources may also have less ability to monitor suspicious activity around the clock.

Foreign governments have already shown interest in those weak spots. CyberGuy previously reported how Chinese hackers gained access to critical American systems, including infrastructure connected to water and energy. The attacker may change. The underlying weakness often looks familiar: exposed equipment, outdated technology or remote access that lacks strong protection.
Could a cyberattack make drinking water unsafe?

A cyberattack against a water utility does not automatically mean the water has been contaminated. In Minnesota, officials reported no known impact on drinking water quality. They also told residents in publicly identified communities that normal water use could continue.

However, a successful attack can cause more serious consequences. The EPA warns that hackers could disrupt treatment or damage equipment. In a worst-case situation, attackers might also interfere with processes that protect water quality.

Manual operations can provide an important safety net. Minnesota workers used those procedures to keep systems running while investigators examined affected technology. Still, a manual backup only helps when employees know how to use it. Utilities need to test those procedures before screens go dark and alarms stop reporting correctly.
How CISA says water utilities should strengthen security

CISA published new international guidance on July 28 called "CI Fortify: Advice for Isolating Vital Systems." The guidance urges critical infrastructure operators to separate vital operational technology from less trusted networks. That isolation can help an essential service continue operating when another part of the organization becomes compromised.

CISA released the guidance on the same day MNIT publicly announced the statewide attack. However, the agency has not said it created the document in response to Minnesota. For water utilities, stronger protection may begin with removing unnecessary internet exposure. When remote access remains necessary, CISA advises placing security controls in front of programmable controllers.

Utilities should also change factory passwords and give employees separate login credentials. EPA inspectors have found water systems that continued using default passwords. Inspectors also discovered shared staff accounts or access that remained active after employees left.

Another EPA finding needs careful context. The agency says more than 70% of inspected systems violated basic federal risk assessment or emergency response planning requirements. That figure does not mean 70% had confirmed cybersecurity breaches. However, inspectors found serious digital security weaknesses at some of those facilities.
TRUMP REJECTS IRAN BLAME FOR MINNESOTA CYBERATTACK, POINTS FINGER AT 'CORRUPT' POLITICAL FOE
Hackers targeted computerized controls at more than 30 Minnesota water systems, forcing some utilities to use manual operations and backup procedures. (Tony Webster/Wikimedia Commons)
What to do if your water utility reports a cyberattack
Residents cannot secure a municipal treatment plant themselves. However, a few steps can help you receive reliable information and avoid scams during an incident.

Check your city, county health department or water utility website for updates. Officials will tell you whether you need to reduce water use or boil tap water. Avoid making decisions based on an unverified neighborhood post.

A cyberattack may affect communications or automated equipment without changing water quality. Continue normal use unless local officials provide different instructions. However, follow any boil-water notice immediately if one appears.

Your city may use text messages, automated calls or government phone alerts during a service disruption. Take a moment to check the emergency alert settings on your iPhone or Android. Also, sign up for your city's local notification system if one is available.

A backup supply can help during any water interruption, whether it begins with a cyberattack or equipment failure. The CDC recommends storing at least one gallon of water per person each day for three days. Households may need more for pets or people with medical needs.

Scammers often take advantage of outages and breaking news. You may receive a message claiming that your water bill failed or that your service will be disconnected. Another message may offer bottled water assistance through a payment link. Do not use the phone number or link inside an unexpected message. Instead, contact the utility through its official website or the number printed on your bill. CyberGuy has also explained how scammers impersonate water and other utility companies by spoofing familiar phone numbers.
Kurt's key takeaways

Minnesota contained a troubling attack without a known drinking water emergency. Workers restored Braham's plant while other utilities relied on manual controls or contingency procedures. However, the number of systems targeted should get the attention of every governor and mayor in America. Hackers apparently found a way to reach dozens of local utilities during the same two-day period. The preliminary suspicion involving Iranian hackers also raises the stakes. Still, investigators need more evidence before anyone treats that attribution as settled. Every community should know which water controls face the internet and whether workers can operate essential equipment manually. States should also help smaller towns that cannot afford their own cybersecurity teams.

title: New York school pauses humanoid classroom robot pilot program
summary: Salamanca City Central School District paid $57,590 for a Realbotix M-Series humanoid robot and AI program that was meant to launch in fall 2026 classrooms.
story: Salamanca High School in New York introduces Sally, a 5'2" humanoid robot, as a teaching assistant for upper grades. Sally features lifelike silicone skin and designed facial expressions. The school district emphasizes that the $57,000 robot won't replace human teachers and operates on a closed AI system with no student data transmitted to manufacturers.

A lifelike humanoid robot was expected to take a seat inside a New York high school classroom. Those plans are now on hold. The planned robot is reportedly stationary, with silicone skin and long brown hair.

Realbotix and Salamanca City Central School District had announced a limited pilot program for fall 2026 involving Optio, an artificial intelligence-powered  educational assistant, and one new Realbotix M-Series humanoid unit.
On July 24, the district announced that the pilot program had been paused while it works through enhanced student data privacy agreements with the New York State Education Department.

The district is also continuing discussions with community members and other stakeholders before moving forward. It has not announced a new date for the pilot program. The technology was intended to support AI and robotics lessons while teachers remained in control. Still, putting a humanlike machine in front of students raises questions about privacy and how quickly students may trust it.

FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS
Salamanca City Central School District will pilot Realbotix’s Optio platform and a purpose-built M-Series humanoid robot in AI and robotics courses. (Jim Shannon/Connecticut Post/Getty Images)
Why Salamanca is testing a humanoid robot in the classroom

Salamanca City Central School District is located in western New York on Seneca Nation territory. The district had planned to introduce Optio to high school students enrolled in Woz ED AI and Robotics courses.

Realbotix previously described this as a limited fall 2026 pilot involving its digital assistant and one physical robot. The district has since placed the project on hold while it addresses student privacy agreements and gathers additional community input. Realbotix told CyberGuy, "The partnership also gives educators an opportunity to evaluate these technologies in a controlled classroom environment under district oversight."

The district reportedly paid $57,590 for the robot and AI program, according to the school board contract. Realbotix reportedly discounted the package from the M-Series robot's listed starting price of $95,000. The initial Optio rollout had been expected to expand to approximately 500 high school students during the fall semester. That planned expansion would have applied to the AI platform and student avatars rather than 500 physical robots.
How the Realbotix classroom robot could work if the pilot resumes

The proposed project includes two connected parts. Optio is the digital AI educational assistant that students can access through personalized avatars. The M-Series robot would give that technology a physical presence in the classroom. Realbotix told CyberGuy, "Its technology combines conversational AI with a physical humanoid platform capable of natural interaction and lifelike expressions."

The company says its humanoid platform can use natural conversation and facial expressions during real-time interactions. The robot is designed to give students hands-on exposure to AI and robotics rather than limiting the lesson to a laptop screen.

The robot was expected to remain seated while using upper-body movements and facial expressions. The school reportedly requested a Western New York accent. However, Realbotix told CyberGuy, "The physical unit has not yet been deployed. Additional details regarding its implementation will be determined in coordination with the district."

That means some details reported about the robot may reflect the planned design rather than the finished classroom robot. The district had said the system would use school-approved curriculum instead of searching the open internet. When the technology lacked an answer, it was trained to say, "I don't know," rather than inventing information.
EDUCATORS WARN AI DEBATE HAS FOCUSED TOO MUCH ON CHEATING, NOT ENOUGH ON STUDENT LEARNING
The $57,590 pilot program could give about 500 high school students access to AI-powered avatars, while one physical humanoid robot serves as a classroom learning tool. (iStock)
What Optio could do for students and teachers

Realbotix designed Optio as an AI educational assistant and an at-home tutor. Students will interact with avatars trained on district curriculum. The platform is designed to reinforce concepts and provide individual tutoring outside regular school hours. Realbotix says it can also offer homework support across multiple languages.

Students reportedly may be able to upload photos of homework for feedback. They could also request lessons based on their interests or receive real-time translations. Teachers may use Optio for lesson planning and curriculum adjustments. The physical robot could also provide prompts based on material already loaded into the system.

Realbotix told CyberGuy, "The program is intended to complement, not replace, teachers by giving students supervised access to emerging AI and robotics tools as part of the district's existing STEM curriculum." The company added, "Realbotix's products are designed to support human engagement and expand access to information and services while complementing the work of educators and other professionals."
How Salamanca plans to protect student privacy

The district has paused the pilot program while it works through enhanced student data privacy agreements with the New York State Education Department. It says appropriate privacy protections and community input are important parts of the process. The district has not said when those agreements could be completed or when the pilot might resume.

If the program moves forward, it would operate under district oversight with education-specific safeguards. Realbotix says those guardrails are designed to block inappropriate responses and reduce unreliable outputs. The robot and avatar would reportedly operate through a closed system without an open internet connection. The district also said Realbotix will lack access to personally identifiable student information.

The classroom robot would reportedly lack facial recognition and recording features found in some other Realbotix models. However, personalized learning requires the system to remember some information. Students will use unique identification codes when interacting with the technology. Those codes will allow Optio to retrieve learning information and continue earlier conversations without relying on a student's name.
What Realbotix says about its corporate structure
Several media reports connected the school project to an adult-products business under the same parent company. Realbotix disputes the way some reports characterized that relationship.
Realbotix provided this clarification to CyberGuy:

"For clarity, some media reports have falsely connected the Salamanca project to an adult product or adult-products business. The Salamanca robot is a newly manufactured, purpose-built educational unit; no existing product or hardware is being modified or repurposed for the school." The company continued, "Realbotix LLC focuses exclusively on non-adult commercial applications, including healthcare and education. No adult-products company has any involvement in the Salamanca project or in any product or project developed by Realbotix LLC. Separate companies."

Realbotix Corp. describes itself as a holding company with two separately operated businesses. Realbotix LLC develops humanoid robots for commercial uses, while Intima LLC operates in the adult wellness and companionship market. The company says the subsidiaries maintain separate employees and facilities. It also says they do not share products, inventory, manufacturing resources or technology. Realbotix told CyberGuy, "The Salamanca robot is a newly manufactured, purpose-built educational unit; no existing product or hardware is being modified or repurposed for the school."
STUDY FINDS MORE AI PRAISE FOR BLACK STUDENTS, SOFTER TREATMENT OF FEMALES
A New York high school plans to test an AI educational assistant and a lifelike humanoid robot under teacher supervision in fall 2026. (Jeffrey Basinger/Newsday RM via Getty Images))
What this means to you

Most students and teachers will not see a humanoid robot in the classroom anytime soon. Still, Salamanca's paused pilot shows where school technology may eventually be heading. Giving AI a face and a voice could make lessons more engaging. It could also lead students to trust the technology more quickly than they would trust a typical computer program.

Parents should pay close attention to what Optio remembers and who can access that information. Teacher oversight will also be important when the system gives an answer that sounds confident but may be wrong. A closed system would give the district more control than an open chatbot. Even so, students, teachers and parents deserve clear rules about student data and how the robot will be used.

The physical unit has yet to enter the school, and the district has not announced a new start date. Before moving forward, Salamanca says it will work through enhanced student data privacy agreements with the New York State Education Department and continue engaging with community members and other stakeholders. Many key questions will remain unanswered until those protections are finalized and students and teachers begin using the system in a real classroom.
Kurt's key takeaways

Pausing the pilot program makes sense while the district works through student privacy agreements. The robot could make AI lessons more engaging, but families still need clear answers about what Optio remembers, who can access that data and when the district deletes it. The real test will come if the district restarts the pilot and shows that the technology can support learning without putting student privacy at risk.
Would you feel comfortable with a lifelike robot helping in your child's classroom, or does this take school technology too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
