Before the revamped edition airs, Season 30 of “The Voice” — with returning coaches Adam Levine and Kelly Clarkson and newcomers Queen Latifah and country music singer Riley Green — will premiere on Sept. 21.
Read on to learn more about “The Voice: Celebrity,” coming in 2027.
Who Will Host ‘The Voice: Celebrity’?
Giving host Carson Daly a break for this celebrity edition is Keke Palmer. The multi-hyphenate will take the helm, bringing her charisma and energy to “The Voice” stage.
Who Are the Coaches for ‘The Voice: Celebrity’?

“The Voice: Celebrity” will have Joe Jonas making his coaching debut this season. He will be joined by Queen Latifah and Riley Green, who will be returning to their red chairs after participating in Season 30.
Who are the Celebrities Competing on ‘The Voice: Celebrity’?
The celebrities that will be part of the inaugural “The Voice: Celebrity” will be revealed at a later time.
However, NBC shared that the stars competing will be actors, musicians, influencers, athletes, comedians and reality television stars.
What Is the New Format for ‘The Voice: Celebrity’?
“The Voice: Celebrity” will follow the same format as the original “The Voice.” The contestants will participate in the blind auditions, hoping for a coach to turn their chair.
They will then be placed into teams and mentored by their coaches to try and make it to the next round as viewers vote for their favorites.
When Does ‘The Voice: Celebrity’ Premiere?
A premiere date has yet to be announced, but expect to see “The Voice: Celebrity” in 2027.

title: Hannah Einbinder Challenges Jenna to a Scream-Off on TODAY
summary: Hannah Einbinder just schooled Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones on the art of screaming.
story: Hannah Einbinder just schooled Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones on the art of screaming.

The actor got a lot of practice letting out her inner rage while filming her new movie “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” and she was happy to share some tricks of the trade while appearing on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle Aug. 4.
During the interview, Jenna complimented Einbinder on her screaming abilities, calling her a “scream queen.”
To develop her screaming skills, Einbinder said she went to a Reiki healer.
“Did you know you were blocked there?” Jenna asked.
“I didn’t. I just feel like as a person, I experienced anger and immediately it turned to sadness. Like I wasn’t able to really exercise my rage,” Einbinder said.
Sheinelle, who admitted that she’s never really been able to scream, was curious to know if Einbinder thinks screaming helps release pent up anger.
“I do,” Einbinder said. “And I think if you find it hard to really scream, that’s also information to perhaps kind of ask why you don’t have access to that part of your voice.”
After undergoing vocal chord surgery, Sheinelle didn’t attempt to scream, but Jenna was up for an exercise with Einbinder.
“I’m perimenopausal so the rage is just (there),” Jenna joked.
Einbinder encouraged viewers to join in and instructed Jenna on how to let out her inner rage.
“We’re gonna take a deep breath in and out, and then another deep breath in, and then we’re gonna let it rock,” she said.
When the time came to scream, Jenna began to join Einbinder, but was overshadowed by the actor’s guttural sound. Sheinelle covered her ears to block out the noise.
The co-hosts were left speechless. Sheinelle and a few crew members applauded Einbinder.
“Feels like I’m the only one who did it,” the actor teased. “It feels like y’all were gonna do it with me.”
“Your scream was so (impressive). I had to live in her scream. I was starting and then I just opened my mouth and let your words come out of me,” Jenna said.
At least the exercise paid off for Einbinder.
“I have to tell you, I feel amazing,” she said.

title: Student kills 6 at school after shooting grandparents in Thailand
summary: ]At least one teacher was killed and four other people injured by a student who opened fire at a school in Thailand on Friday before killing himself, authorities said.
story: BANGKOK — A gunman shot and killed his grandparents before killing six people and himself at a school outside Bangkok on Friday, authorities in Thailand said, in the Southeast Asian nation’s worst mass killing since 2022.

Three teachers and three students were killed in the shooting at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in the Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province, north of Bangkok, according to police. At least 15 others were injured, including two in critical condition.

Police said the gunman, whom they identified as a student, had fired at least 26 rounds and that 34 other rounds of ammunition were found at the scene. They said they had recovered a 9mm handgun believed to belong to his grandfather.
One 18-year-old student told Reuters that at first he thought he was hearing firecrackers.
“Then it started getting more frequent, like ‘bang, bang, bang’ and then it went quiet at one point,” the unnamed student said. “And the shooting started again.”
In a statement, the school said the shooting had “shaken the hearts” of students, parents, teachers and others.
The government said Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul had directed relevant agencies to provide immediate and comprehensive support to all those affected.

“We rushed to care for the injured and I have dispatched the relevant personnel to handle the situation at the site,” he told reporters. “This is very terrible, it is something that should not have happened.”
It is the second school shooting in Thailand this year.
One teacher was killed and a student was injured in February at a school in the southern district of Hat Yai.
In recent years there has been a series of deadly shootings at schools and other locations in Thailand, where gun ownership is common.
Last year, six people were killed when a man opened fire at a Bangkok market before taking his own life.
In 2023, a 14-year-old killed two people and injured five others in a shooting at a luxury mall in Bangkok.

The previous year, a former police officer killed 36 people during a three-hour shooting and stabbing spree in the country’s northeast. Among his victims were 22 children he stabbed at a day care center.
A Thai soldier also killed 29 people in a shooting rampage in the northeastern city of Nakhon Ratchasima in 2020.

After the 2023 mall shooting, Anutin, who was interior minister at the time, enacted a one-year ban on the issue of new personal gun licenses and suspended public carry permits, among other gun control measures. The suspension of public carry permits was extended earlier this year.
“This is the reason why the government doesn’t allow arm carrying and extension of gun licenses,” Anutin said Friday. “This is the reason why.”

As of 2017 Thai civilians were estimated to possess about 10.3 million firearms, or about 15 per 100 residents, according to the Small Arms Survey, a Swiss group that favors gun control. That compared with more than 393 million firearms in civilian possession in the United States, or 120.5 per 100 residents.
Nat Sumon reported from Bangkok, and Jennifer Jett from Hong Kong.

title: Trump administration revokes Brazilian ambassador’s visa in diplomatic dispute
summary: The Trump administration revoked the visa of Brazil’s U.S. ambassador Tuesday — the latest jab in a monthslong diplomatic spat between the two countries.
story: The Trump administration revoked the visa of Brazil’s U.S. ambassador Tuesday — the latest jab in a monthslong diplomatic spat between the two countries.

The U.S. action was taken in retaliation for Brazil’s withholding formal approval for the Trump administration’s pick for U.S. ambassador to Brazil, Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez, a senior State Department official told reporters Tuesday.
The official, who spoke on behalf of the State Department on condition of anonymity, said Brazil has indicated the approval is likely to be delayed until after its election in October.
The Brazilian government said it repudiates the visa revocation of their ambassador, calling both justifications from the U.S. “false,” and noted that the U.S. request remains under review.

“It should be recalled that individual sanctions against Brazilian officials remain in force, notably the cancellation of U.S. visas based on the unfounded allegation that former President Bolsonaro is being subjected to political persecution,” the office of the president of Brazil said in a statement. “Those affected include Supreme Court justices and senior members of the Executive Branch.”
Jair Bolsonaro was the president of Brazil before President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The Brazilian president’s office said the decision “is not an isolated incident,” and “forms part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, driven by ideological motives that are incompatible with a bilateral partnership that has always been guided by mutual respect.”

The tit-for-tat has been ongoing since at least March, when Brazil denied visas to a U.S. delegation traveling to a critical minerals forum, the U.S. official said. In July, Brazil also denied visas to two U.S. officials, accusing them of plotting to meddle in Brazil’s electoral process.
“This week we had to deny visas to two young folks they were sending to Brazil to meddle in Brazil’s elections,” Lula said at an event last Wednesday.

The senior State Department official denied the accusations and said the assistant secretary for democracy, human rights and labor, Riley M. Barnes, and one of his deputies, Samuel Samson, “were making a routine trip” and were “denied the ability to do routine, common work between the two countries.”

“We’ve taken reciprocal action with respect to the Brazilian diplomat here to make the point that it can’t always be one-sided,” the senior State Department official said. “If there’s going to be limitations on one side’s diplomats, they will be reciprocated.”

The official clarified that Brazilian Ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti will not be expelled from the U.S. but warned that additional diplomatic options remain on the table if the Brazilian government continues to delay or refuse to approve the U.S. ambassador nominee. If Viotti leaves the country, she would need to reapply for a visa, the official said, adding that the Brazilian ambassador’s visa will be reinstated if Brazil approves Perez.

“We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” the official said. “President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world.”

“President Trump is assembling an America First diplomatic A-team across his administration, subject to the advice and consent of the Senate. We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes,” the official added.

title: Trump claims Iran talks are underway as Tehran denies it
summary: The international oil benchmark Brent crude rose again to 2.7% with traffic through the crucial waterway at a trickle compared with its peacetime flow.
story: President Donald Trump accused Iran of duplicity and insisted the two sides were discussing reopening the Strait of Hormuz as early as Tuesday, even as Tehran denied talks were even taking place.

The diplomatic confusion was underscored by an attack on a cargo vessel near the strait’s Oman coast, as reported by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, an organization run by the British navy that helps protect commercial shipping in high-risk areas.

With traffic through the bottleneck still at a trickle of its peacetime flow, the international oil benchmark Brent crude rose again by 2.7% Tuesday, reflecting uncertainty in the market rather than any confidence in the diplomatic process.

title: Video shows moment drone burst into fireball on Russian beach
summary: Ukraine didn’t deny launching the drone but said the Kremlin’s air defenses had shot it down and that “it was Putin who killed these Russians.”
story: The beach was packed, many vacationers lounging near the turquoise waters when the drone slammed into the white sand and burst into a fireball.

Russian officials said seven people, including three children, were killed and 58 others injured by the explosion in the Black Sea resort town of Gelendzhik on Monday. The explosion was captured on video, which was shared on social media and verified by NBC News.

Moscow accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, which would constitute a war crime, and unleashed a barrage of aerial strikes on its neighbor. Ukraine’s attacks inside Russia come as its own civilians faced deadly Russian bombardment throughout the summer.
Ukrainian officials did not confirm they were responsible, but they also did not deny it.

“What happened today was a deliberate strike by the Kyiv regime against the civilian population — people who have absolutely no connection to military infrastructure,” Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of the Krasnodar region, said on his official Telegram channel. “There can be no justification for such a cynical and inhumane terrorist act targeting children.”

The explosion comes amid a concerted Ukrainian effort to push the war’s front line closer than ever to Moscow, with strikes targeting shipping vessels, oil sites, warehouses and ammunition depots in recent weeks.

Since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Kyiv has honed an innovative and lethal strategy of using cheaply manufactured drones as it seeks to pressure Moscow into a peace settlement. Some hit their targets, while others are often shot down.
Between July 24 and July 31, at least 61 people were killed and more than 320 wounded in Ukrainian shelling and drone strikes, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said Friday.

After the explosion in Gelendzhik, Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukrainian National Security and Defense Council’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said: “Russian air defense shot down a drone onto people lying on the beach.”
“It was Putin who killed these Russians,” he said in a statement. “Had he not started the war and the strikes on Ukraine, they would be alive.”
Kovalenko also accused Putin of downplaying Ukrainian attacks on Russia, creating an “illusion of peace” that has made the public complacent.
“Had they acknowledged the war on their own territory, people would have reacted more actively to the alert, which in some places in Russia is not even announced,” he said.
A separate attack had also hit a warehouse in Leningrad, its regional governor, Aleksandr Drozdenko, said early Tuesday.

title: East Asia is baking in ‘cruelly hot’ summer
summary: A deadly heat wave is gripping large parts of East Asia, bringing the hottest temperature on record in South Korea and complicating earthquake recovery efforts in Japan.
story: A deadly heat wave is gripping large parts of East Asia, bringing the hottest temperature on record in South Korea and complicating earthquake recovery efforts in Japan.
Extreme heat has been linked to 19 deaths in South Korea since mid-May, with President Lee Jae Myung calling it a national disaster Tuesday.
“We need to make efforts for ​a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, ‌since this extreme weather is becoming normal,” he said at a Cabinet meeting.
On Sunday, temperatures hit 42.5 degrees Celsius (108 degrees Fahrenheit) in the southeastern city of Yangsan, the highest in 122 years of record-keeping.

title: Trump calls Iranian leadership ‘extremely duplicitous’ after Tehran denies new talks will start Monday
summary: Iran said it wasn’t holding talks with the U.S. but was in discussions with Oman over a temporary safe route through the Strait of Hormuz.
story: President Donald Trump branded the Iranian regime “unbelievably duplicitous,” saying Iranian officials asked for talks on ending the war only to announce that no discussions would be held.

Trump had earlier said that the United States and Iran will hold new discussions Monday afternoon, after he called off intense new strikes to allow for a deal on the Strait of Hormuz and Tehran’s nuclear program.
However, Iran said it was not holding talks with the U.S. but was in discussions with Oman over a temporary safe route through the strait.

“We currently do not have negotiations with America,” and Iran has no plans to host foreign delegations or send negotiators abroad in the coming days, Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters.

Trump later took to Truth Social, where he wrote: “Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous! They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg,’ talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman.’”
Iran did not immediately respond to his comments.
Trump later told reporters at the White House after his post on Truth Social that talks with Iran were taking place.

“They’re going on right now. It’s an amazing thing we have a little problem with Iran because we have many talks, and we’ll say we have or we don’t have. You know, we’re straight about it, but they deny it,” Trump said. “But they’re not denying it now. They just put out a statement not denying it.”
Trump also told reporters that the Strait of Hormuz will be open to marine traffic Tuesday.

“We’re talking about the strait, the opening of the strait, having it open literally by tomorrow, completely open, and that’s phase one,” Trump said, saying the second phase of talks would focus on Iran’s nuclear program.
Time is running out for Iran to make a deal, according to Trump.
“This is a last chance for them to sign a good document,” Trump said, adding, “I want to give them every last chance before decapitation.”
Trump had said Sunday that he agreed to call off the attacks amid what he said were the “parameters of a deal” that would include resuming shipping through the key global trade route.

Speaking on Air Force One, Trump said the canceled strikes were going to be “the biggest attack since World War II.” The president said that the U.S. was “holding” what would have been a “massive attack,” but that it could still take place “anytime we want.”
Trump, however, said that Iran does not have a deadline to come to an agreement.

title: U.S. agrees to pause attacks on Iran subject to ‘rapidly’ making deal, Trump says
summary: The deal would include reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending Tehran’s “nuclear threat,” the president said.
story: The U.S. has agreed to pause attacks on Iran, President Donald Trump said Saturday, amid what he said were the “perimeters of a deal” that would include the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s  nuclear threat.”
The president said the U.S. was “locked and loaded and ready to go” but that he agreed to cancel attacks “subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”
He added that Israel, the U.S. partner in the war with Iran, “joins me in this commitment.”
“Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE,” Trump said of a possible new agreement.

The statement came after the State Department on Saturday urged Americans across the Middle East to consider leaving the region or be prepared to depart on short notice. It also warned of flight disruptions and security risks as the conflict with Iran appeared to be escalating.

Trump earlier threatened Iran with additional attacks, saying Friday that the U.S. will be “hitting them very hard,” while Iran has vowed to “punish” the U.S. and both nations traded what some U.S. officials described as “heavy” strikes.
Responding to Trump’s announcement, Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told “Meet the Press” Sunday that the president should not trust Iran’s word.
Asked why a fresh deal would be different when the memorandum of understanding signed in June failed, he told moderator Kristen Welker: “Well, it may not be.”
“We only have three choices: escalate, retreat and come home, or maintain the status quo. I would maintain the status quo as long as I could,” he said.
Iran’s acting minister of defense, Majid Ibn al-Reza, meanwhile said that U.S. remarks should be viewed as “psychological and cognitive warfare.”
He said on X that the threat of further strikes would be taken “as the basis for increasing readiness, strengthening deterrence, and enhancing our own power.”

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, a key regional player, spoke with Trump by phone Saturday. According to the Saudi state news agency, he told him that dialogue was needed to de-escalate Middle East tensions, and expressed concerns over plans for new strikes against Iran.
The State Department issued fresh security guidance Saturday for Americans in the region.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” the State Department said. “Some airlines in the region have postponed resumption of earlier flight schedules; others have cancelled some routes. Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation.”
The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel bans to or through the region.
The warning was distributed through U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

The agency posted a nearly identical statement earlier this month, but that bulletin did not urge Americans to prepare to leave the Middle East or to reconsider upcoming trips, reflecting Washington’s growing concern that the conflict could widen.
On Saturday, the Kuwait army said its air defense systems intercepted drone attacks from Iran.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently engaging hostile drone attacks following the Iranian aggression. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosions heard are a result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks,” the army said.

Earlier in the week, the U.S. military confirmed it had executed a “heavy wave of strikes” on Iran, hours after Fox News reported that the president in a phone call had vowed to “beat the f-----g s--- out of” the country.
Trump has grown increasingly exasperated with the state of the war, one Trump ally told NBC News.
“There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint,” the ally said.
The conflict has now entered its sixth month, despite Trump’s repeated early predictions that the war would resolve itself “shortly.”
The protracted conflict has led to soaring oil prices globally and rising gas prices in the U.S.
There was a brief reprieve from fighting in June when the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding outlining the process for talks to end the war.
But in early July, Trump declared a ceasefire to be “over,” and the countries resumed striking targets in the Middle East.
